2026-06-12 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of three now-patched security flaws impacting LangGraph, including a critical vulnerability chain that could result in remote code execution. LangGraph is an open-source framework created by LangChain to build complex, stateful, and multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) agentic applications. LangGraph get_state_history SQLi via metadata filter (CVE-2025-67644) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to a self-hosted LangGraph server's get_state_history endpoint where the metadata filter parameter carries SQL injection syntax. Targets the first step of the published RCE chain — manipulating the SQLite checkpoint query to return an attacker-controlled BLOB. Rationale: Article explicitly names the get_state_history() endpoint and identifies CVE-2025-67644 as a SQLi in metadata filter keys against the SQLite checkpointer. The URL-substring set covers union-based and tautology payloads that any working exploit would emit. defender_kql is empty because Defender Advanced Hunting has no inbound HTTP request body table; sentinel ImWebSession is the right pivot.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanner runs (Burp, sqlmap, internal DAST) hitting LangGraph endpoints
  • Developers debugging the get_state_history endpoint with literal SQL keywords in filter strings
  • Pen-testing engagements with documented scope
  • Test fixtures that embed UNION/SELECT in payloads stored as filter values
  • Web spider crawling the LangGraph admin UI
Suppression filter
and SrcIpAddr !in ("<scanner_ip_1>", "<scanner_ip_2>") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("sqlmap", "Burp", "ZAP")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is not an approved scanner/pen-test source; pull the full request URL, body, response status and any subsequent process spawned by the LangGraph runtime within 30s on the target host. 2) Contain: if status was 200 and the runtime PID then forked a shell/curl/wget (see UC2), isolate the host via MDE LiveResponse and snapshot the SQLite checkpoint DB before it is overwritten. 3) Hunt: pivot the source IP across ImWebSession for any other LangGraph endpoints touched in the last 30 days; review checkpoints table for rows whose metadata column contains opcode markers (\x80, \x95) suggesting an injected msgpack BLOB.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "get_state_history"
| where Url has "filter"
| where Url has_any ("UNION", "SELECT", "%27", "--", "DROP", "sqlite_master", "%20OR%20", "%20AND%20")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Shell/LOLBin spawned by LangGraph Python or Node runtime AIInstallation High
Detects classic post-RCE behaviour where a LangGraph runtime process (python/uvicorn/node executing a langgraph entrypoint) spawns a shell or download utility. Anchors to parent command lines containing langgraph/langchain/checkpoint so it does not fire on generic python workloads. Rationale: Article describes RCE achieved after chained SQLi+deserialization where the malicious msgpack payload runs in the LangGraph application runtime. Anchoring on python/uvicorn/node parents with langgraph/langchain/checkpoint/get_state_history in the parent cmdline keeps this from firing on generic dev environments. The LOLBin child set is the standard post-exec pivot.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientists running interactive notebooks that shell out via subprocess from a langchain pipeline
  • CI jobs in langgraph repos invoking shell during tests or build
  • Custom langgraph tools that legitimately wrap curl/bash (web-fetch, k8s exec tooling)
  • Operators running troubleshooting commands inside a running uvicorn container via docker exec — parent reparented to python
  • langgraph-cli launching helper utilities like git or pip during package install
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langgraph-cli", "langgraph dev", "langgraph build") and FileName in~ ("git.exe", "pip.exe", "pip3"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ParentCommandLine + ChildCmd, confirm the LangGraph server PID's listening port and whether get_state_history was hit in the last 5 minutes (cross-reference UC1). Check whether the child command line includes base64, /dev/tcp/, or python -c — strong RCE signal. 2) Contain: isolate the host via MDE LiveResponse, dump the running python process memory (procdump) to preserve the deserialized payload, kill the runtime PID. 3) Hunt: search for any FileWritten by the same PID in the prior 60 minutes (UC5), enumerate other hosts running the same langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite version (UC3) and any outbound network the runtime opened (UC4).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langgraph","langchain","checkpoint","get_state_history")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash.exe","sh","bash","curl.exe","wget.exe","curl","wget","nc","ncat.exe","certutil.exe","chmod","chmod.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","node")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("langgraph","langchain","checkpoint","get_state_history")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langgraph","langchain","checkpoint","get_state_history")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh","cmd.exe","bash","sh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","certutil.exe","chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\uvicorn.exe OR *\\node.exe) (@ParentCommandLine:*langgraph* OR @ParentCommandLine:*langchain* OR @ParentCommandLine:*checkpoint* OR @ParentCommandLine:*get_state_history*) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\bash.exe OR *\\sh.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\certutil.exe)

Vulnerable langgraph / langgraph-checkpoint package version inventory AIReconnaissance High
Enumerates hosts running langgraph, langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite or @langchain/langgraph-checkpoint-redis at a version below the published fix. Lets the SOC quantify exposure to CVE-2025-67644, CVE-2026-28277 and CVE-2026-27022 before applying compensating controls. Rationale: Article supplies the exact fixed-version thresholds: langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite < 3.0.1, langgraph < 1.0.10, @langchain/langgraph-checkpoint-redis < 1.0.1. The regex ranges encode those exactly. The cross-join with DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing prioritises the highest-risk surface (self-hosted, internet-exposed) which is the scope the article calls out as affected.
ATT&CKT1592.002
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped/internal-only test hosts running an old langgraph for replay
  • Forks/vendored copies of langgraph whose internal version string drops the upstream version
  • CI build agents that briefly install old langgraph for regression tests
  • Docker base images with langgraph baked in but no exposed get_state_history endpoint
  • Hosts running langgraph-checkpoint-postgres (not vulnerable) but a stale langgraph package
Response runbook
1) Triage: enrich each vulnerable host with internet-exposure (IsInternetFacing), whether the LangGraph server listens on a non-loopback port, and whether anonymous access to get_state_history is permitted. 2) Contain: for any internet-exposed host running the SQLite or Redis checkpointer, force-upgrade to the fixed versions (langgraph >=1.0.10, langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite >=3.0.1, @langchain/langgraph-checkpoint-redis >=1.0.1) and rotate any runtime secrets the agent could read. 3) Hunt: replay 30 days of UC1 (SQLi probe) and UC2 (shell from runtime) against the exposed host set to look for prior exploitation; check checkpoint table for rows whose metadata column carries msgpack opcode prefixes.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "langgraph"
| extend Vulnerable = case(
    SoftwareName has "langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite" and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^([0-2]\.|3\.0\.0$)", "CVE-2025-67644",
    SoftwareName has "langgraph-checkpoint-redis"  and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(0\.|1\.0\.0$)",   "CVE-2026-27022",
    SoftwareName == "langgraph"                    and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^1\.0\.[0-9]$",     "CVE-2026-28277",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Vulnerable)
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, Vulnerable
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId in ("CVE-2025-67644","CVE-2026-28277","CVE-2026-27022")
   or (SoftwareName has "langgraph" and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^1\.0\.[0-9]$")
   or (SoftwareName has "langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite" and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^([0-2]\.|3\.0\.0$)")
   or (SoftwareName has "langgraph-checkpoint-redis" and SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^(0\.|1\.0\.0$)")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, OSVersion, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2025-67644","CVE-2026-28277","CVE-2026-27022") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.cve Vulnerabilities.severity Vulnerabilities.cvss
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - cvss
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Vulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve IN ("CVE-2025-67644","CVE-2026-28277","CVE-2026-27022") by Vulnerabilities.dest Vulnerabilities.signature Vulnerabilities.cve Vulnerabilities.severity Vulnerabilities.cvss
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Outbound public network from LangGraph runtime to non-allowlisted destination AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts public-internet egress from a LangGraph runtime process (python/uvicorn/node) to a destination outside the standard AI-API / package-registry allowlist. Catches C2 callback or exfiltration after RCE via the CVE chain. Rationale: Article frames exploitation as RCE on the LangGraph host runtime — successful RCE almost always pivots to outbound C2 or secret exfiltration. Article maintainers themselves warn the runtime can 'expose runtime secrets or provide access to other systems'. The python/uvicorn/node parent set scopes to the runtime; the allowlist of LLM-API and Python-registry FQDNs eliminates the usual legitimate traffic. Sentinel query relies on host-name tagging since ImNetworkSession lacks a process-name column in the canonical schema — operators must tag LangGraph hosts accordingly or supplement with an ASIM parser that joins process context.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LangGraph tools that fetch from arbitrary websites as part of a research agent's tool-use
  • Telemetry / APM agents bundled inside the python runtime calling out to Datadog/Sentry/NewRelic
  • HuggingFace Hub mirror configured to a corporate proxy hostname
  • Webhook-style tools posting to Slack/Discord/Teams
  • First-run of a langgraph deployment downloading model artifacts from a non-listed CDN
Suppression filter
and DstHostname !endswith "datadoghq.com" and DstHostname !endswith "sentry.io" and DstHostname !endswith "newrelic.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination is not a corporate-approved 3rd-party (Datadog, Sentry, custom HF mirror); pull DNS history for the destination and any threat-intel reputation; check whether the same runtime PID also spawned a shell (UC2) or wrote files (UC5) inside the same hour. 2) Contain: block the destination FQDN/IP at the egress proxy/firewall, then isolate the host via MDE LiveResponse; rotate any API tokens reachable from the runtime environment. 3) Hunt: pivot the destination IP across other tenants for similar tool-runtime-to-IP traffic; sweep langgraph hosts (UC3) for matching outbound to the same destination.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langgraph","langchain","checkpoint")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteUrl !endswith "pypi.org"
   and RemoteUrl !endswith "files.pythonhosted.org"
   and RemoteUrl !endswith "openai.com"
   and RemoteUrl !endswith "anthropic.com"
   and RemoteUrl !endswith "huggingface.co"
   and RemoteUrl !endswith "githubusercontent.com"
   and RemoteUrl !endswith "github.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SrcHostname has_any ("langgraph","agent","ai-agent","llm")
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.16."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.17."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.18."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.19."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.20."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.21."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.22."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.23."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.24."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.25."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.26."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.27."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.28."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.29."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.30."
   and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.31."
   and DstIpAddr != "127.0.0.1"
| where DstHostname !endswith "pypi.org"
   and DstHostname !endswith "pythonhosted.org"
   and DstHostname !endswith "openai.com"
   and DstHostname !endswith "anthropic.com"
   and DstHostname !endswith "huggingface.co"
   and DstHostname !endswith "githubusercontent.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File writes to sensitive paths by LangGraph Python/Node runtime AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects post-RCE payload drops where the compromised LangGraph runtime writes to typical persistence/staging locations on Linux (/tmp, /etc/cron, ~/.ssh, dotfiles) or Windows (Startup, ProgramData, Public, Temp). The parent process anchor stops generic python/node file activity from firing. Rationale: Article identifies RCE on the application runtime as the chain's terminal impact, where the maintainers themselves note the agent runtime can 'expose runtime secrets or provide access to other systems'. The path/extension set covers the classic post-RCE staging targets on both Linux (cron, ssh keys, dotfiles, /tmp) and Windows containers running LangGraph (Startup, ProgramData, Temp). The parent-process langgraph/langchain cmdline anchor differentiates from generic Python ML workflows that write to /tmp.
ATT&CKT1105 T1547.001 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • langgraph checkpoint files legitimately written to /tmp during dev runs
  • Pip/uv installs invoked from inside the runtime writing .so/.py files into site-packages under /tmp pip cache
  • Application logs rotated into /var/tmp by the runtime
  • Container-local sqlite checkpoint DB written into /tmp by langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite itself
  • ssh-agent or known_hosts updates by maintenance scripts running in the same container as the agent
Suppression filter
and not (FolderPath has "/tmp/langgraph" and FileName endswith ".sqlite") and not (FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\pip\cache\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped file against threat intel and VirusTotal; check whether it is executable, world-writable, or stored in an autostart path; confirm if the same PID also opened public outbound (UC4) or spawned a shell (UC2) in the same window. 2) Contain: quarantine the dropped file and any copies via MDE LiveResponse, kill the originating PID, and snapshot the host for forensics; if the file is in /etc/cron* or a systemd unit dir, also pull and review the schedule entry. 3) Hunt: across the langgraph host fleet (UC3) search ImFileEvent / DeviceFileEvents for the same SHA256 or filename pattern over the prior 30 days; review checkpoint DB rows touched by the same runtime around the drop time for the original msgpack payload.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","node.exe","node")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langgraph","langchain","checkpoint","get_state_history")
| where (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup", "/tmp/", "/var/tmp/", "/etc/cron", "/root/.ssh/", "/.ssh/", "/etc/systemd/system/"))
   or FileName in~ ("authorized_keys",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc")
   or FileName endswith ".sh" or FileName endswith ".py" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".so"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","pythonw","uvicorn","node")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langgraph","langchain","checkpoint","get_state_history")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/etc/cron","/root/.ssh/","/.ssh/","/etc/systemd/system/",@"\Windows\Temp\",@"\Users\Public\",@"\ProgramData\",@"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("authorized_keys",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc")
   or TargetFileExtension in~ ("sh","py","exe","dll","so","ko")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Sensitive Path File Write by LangGraph Python/Node Runtime
id: 1d4c7b5e-df30-4e6b-ca5c-5c6e7f08192a
description: Detects file creation/modification in common persistence or payload-staging paths originating from a LangGraph runtime process — possible post-RCE behaviour after CVE-2025-67644 + CVE-2026-28277 chain exploitation.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/langgraph-flaw-chain-exposes-self.html
author: SOC
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_process:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\uvicorn.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
  selection_paths:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Windows\Temp\'
      - '\Users\Public\'
      - '\ProgramData\'
      - '\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\uvicorn.exe OR *\\node.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\\Windows\\Temp\\* OR *\\Users\\Public\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\* OR *\\Startup\\* OR *.exe OR *.dll OR *.ps1 OR *.bat)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/(python|python3|pythonw|uvicorn|node)(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(?i)(/tmp/|/var/tmp/|/etc/cron|/root/\\.ssh/|/\\.ssh/authorized_keys|\\\\Windows\\\\Temp\\\\|\\\\Users\\\\Public\\\\|\\\\ProgramData\\\\|\\\\Startup\\\\|\\.bashrc$|\\.bash_profile$|\\.profile$|\\.sh$|\\.exe$|\\.dll$|\\.so$)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3","uvicorn","uvicorn.exe","node.exe","node") AND Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") AND (Filesystem.file_path IN ("*\\Windows\\Temp\\*","*\\Users\\Public\\*","*\\ProgramData\\*","*\\Startup\\*","/tmp/*","/var/tmp/*","/etc/cron*","/root/.ssh/*","*/.ssh/authorized_keys","*/.bashrc","*/.bash_profile","*/.profile")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental

    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")

        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

INTERPOL Operation Takes Down Sniper Dz Phishing Platform, Arrests Administrator

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 12 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An INTERPOL-led operation last month resulted in the disruption of Sniper Dz, a decade-long phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform, Group-IB said Thursday. The effort, codenamed Operation Ramz, took place between October 2025 and February 2026, and saw authorities from 13 countries in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region making 201 arrests. Included among them was Guedz, the primary

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Raviral.com Sniper Dz kit endpoints accessed (k_fac.php / track.js) · [LLM] Phishing email click landing on Sniper Dz infrastructure (URL/click correlation) · [LLM] Brand-impersonating phishing pages on abused free-hosting platforms (Sniper Dz pattern) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Sniper Dz seized phishing infrastructure callback (post-takedown beacons) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Sniper Dz seized phishing infrastructure callback (post-takedown beacons) AICommand & Control High
Hunts internal hosts resolving or connecting to Sniper Dz / Joker Dz infrastructure domains seized during INTERPOL Operation Ramz. Any post-takedown beacon to these domains indicates a pre-existing compromise: dormant malware, browser-stored phishing-page bookmarks being clicked, or a victim whose stolen credentials are still being replayed from a host that's reaching the staging infra. Rationale: All 13 domains are taken verbatim from the article's pre-extracted IOC bundle for Sniper Dz / Joker Dz infrastructure seized by INTERPOL. Any callback to seized infrastructure is high-fidelity because the platform was taken offline in Feb 2026 — legitimate traffic should be zero. Cross-reference with the Group-IB / Unit 42 (Oct 2024) Sniper Dz writeups referenced in the article.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-research sandbox detonation (any.run, Hybrid Analysis worker subnets) resolving seized domains as part of historical sample replay
  • Threat-intel enrichment platforms (Recorded Future, Anomali) doing periodic IOC validation from corporate egress
  • Vulnerability scanners with web-crawl modes hitting the IOC list
  • Researchers / red-teamers replaying old phishing PCAPs in a lab subnet that egresses through corporate proxy
  • Web filters that prefetch / categorize URLs from blocklists they pull themselves
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","smartscreen.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\Windows Defender" and DeviceName !startswith "sandbox-" and DeviceName !startswith "sb-"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the initiating process and parent for the connection on the implicated host. Determine whether it's a browser (user clicked an old bookmark / opened an archived email), a sandbox VM, or an unknown process (likely dormant stealer). Check the host's mail history for the URL. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole all 13 domains at the proxy / DNS resolver immediately; this should be a permanent blocklist. Isolate the host if the calling process is non-browser. Force a password reset for the implicated user across SSO and externally-facing brand accounts (PayPal, Facebook, Steam, Netflix) given the credential-theft objective of the platform. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot the host's AAD sign-in history for the past 90 days against impossible-travel / new-MFA-device events. Sweep the org for any other host that resolved any seized domain in the last 180 days using the same IOC list.

Raviral.com Sniper Dz kit endpoints accessed (k_fac.php / track.js) AIDelivery High
Hunts HTTP/S access to two highly-specific Sniper Dz kit URLs documented by Group-IB: `/k_fac.php` (the Facebook-template credential submission endpoint) and `/host_style/style/js-track/track.js` (the per-victim tracking script). Either path appearing on the wire from an internal host is a strong indicator that a user is sitting on a live Sniper Dz phishing page on the seized infrastructure or a mirror. Rationale: `/k_fac.php` and `/host_style/style/js-track/track.js` are kit-specific filenames pulled from the article's IOC bundle (Group-IB analysis of seized raviral.com hosting). These paths have no legitimate use outside the Sniper Dz Facebook phishing template, so a single hit is high-confidence. Combining path-match with host=raviral.com catches mirrored/cloned kits even if the domain changes.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1056.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A blue-team detonation lab fetching the IOC URL for signature development
  • Researcher pulling the kit source via curl/wget from a workstation behind the corporate proxy
  • An automated phishing-takedown vendor (PhishLabs, Netcraft) scanning from the corporate IP space
  • Mirror-by-coincidence: an unrelated CMS that happens to expose /k_fac.php — verify the Referer / Host pairing
  • Search-engine crawler image rendering of archived screenshots that embed track.js
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("-IOC","--ioc","threat-intel","sandbox")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For the matching host, pull the full browser session — Referer chain, parent process of the browser tab, and the exact URL preceding the kit-path fetch. If the parent is Outlook/Teams/explorer.exe via a link-click, treat as a confirmed live phishing visit. Step 2 (contain): Block raviral.com plus the two kit paths at the egress proxy. Reset the user's credentials for any brand the kit template impersonated (the article lists PayPal, Facebook, Instagram, Yahoo, Netflix, Steam as primary targets — Facebook is the `_fac` template). Revoke active AAD sessions and require MFA re-enrollment. Step 3 (hunt): Search the prior 48h of EmailEvents for any URL pointing at raviral.com or the other 12 seized domains for this recipient, and pivot across all internal users who received the same NetworkMessageId thread.

| order by Timestamp desc

  ( ImWebSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where Url has_any ("/k_fac.php", "/host_style/style/js-track/track.js") or HttpHostName endswith "raviral.com" | project TimeGenerated, Source=EventProduct, Host=SrcHostname, User=SrcUsername, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, MatchedURL=Url, Dest=HttpHostName, Method=HttpMethod, UA=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent )

Phishing email click landing on Sniper Dz infrastructure (URL/click correlation) AIDelivery High
Correlates Defender for O365 Safe-Links click telemetry against the 13 seized Sniper Dz / Joker Dz domains. A `ClickAllowed` or `ClickedThrough` to any of these URLs proves the user reached a credential-harvesting page — a higher-fidelity signal than passive email delivery alone. Rationale: Joins inbound delivered email containing any of the 13 article-listed Sniper Dz domains to a Safe-Links click event proving the user actually reached the credential-capture page. The IOC list is verbatim from the article's pre-extracted bundle. Falcon LogScale left empty: FDR does not ship M365 Defender email/URL-click telemetry.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security awareness training platforms (KnowBe4, Cofense PhishMe) using these domains as decoys in simulated phishing — filter by known campaign sender
  • Threat-intel analysts forwarding phishing samples to a shared mailbox, then clicking from a triage console
  • User submits a phishing report through the Outlook 'Report Phish' button which clicks the URL in a sandboxed renderer
  • Mail with the URL gets archived to a researcher's quarantine inbox and the link is opened from there
  • Press-release / news article that legitimately links to a sniperdz.com forensic summary
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("phishreport@contoso.com","abuse@contoso.com","soc@contoso.com") and IPAddress !in ("<known SOC sandbox egress IP>","<KnowBe4 simulator egress>")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the NetworkMessageId from the click and inspect EmailEvents for sender authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), DeliveryLocation, and whether other recipients in the same thread also clicked. Look up the user's role in IdentityInfo to assess credential-blast-radius. Step 2 (contain): Force a password reset and revoke active sessions for the clicking user via Azure AD. Soft-delete the message from all recipients with Threat Explorer / `Soft-Delete`. Add the matched URL+domain to the tenant block list. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot AADSignInEventsBeta for the clicking user looking for sign-ins within 2-6h of the click from unusual countries / new IPs / non-compliant devices. Sweep EmailEvents for any other inbound mail with URLs to the 12 sibling domains within the last 30d.

Brand-impersonating phishing pages on abused free-hosting platforms (Sniper Dz pattern) AIDelivery Medium
Hunting query for the structural signature of Sniper Dz phishing pages: brand keywords (PayPal, Facebook, Instagram, Netflix, Steam, Yahoo, Free Fire / Garena, PUBG — the named targets in the article) embedded in the subdomain or path of free-hosting platforms (github.io, netlify.app, glitch.me, pantheonsite.io, 000webhostapp.com, epizy.com, blogspot.*). Surfaces unseen Sniper Dz / Joker Dz mirrors that re-spawn after the seizure, plus copycat PhaaS using the same hosting playbook. Rationale: Pattern extracted from the 13 article-listed Sniper Dz IOCs: 8 of them are brand- or lure-keyword subdomains on free hosting (github.io, netlify.app, glitch.me, pantheonsite.io, 000webhostapp.com, epizy.com, blogspot.be). Article says the platform deployed 80 templates across 30 brands in 5 languages and 20,000+ domains have been associated — first-seen hunting against this signature catches mirrors and copycat PhaaS operators using the same playbook.
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate brand-run microsites on Netlify/Vercel (some companies host promo pages this way) — verify by checking SSL cert SAN list
  • Researchers/students publishing fan sites or CTF write-ups containing brand names
  • Open-source projects hosted on GitHub Pages with names that coincidentally include 'login' or 'secure'
  • Legitimate gaming-community sites for Free Fire / PUBG / Garena hosted on free platforms — common in MENA / SEA
  • Brand-protection vendors crawling these patterns from corporate egress
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !startswith "https://docs." and RemoteUrl !startswith "https://help." and RemoteUrl !contains "/issues/" and RemoteUrl !contains "/blob/" and RemoteUrl !contains "/pull/"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each first-seen hit, render the URL in a sandbox and verify it's a credential-capture page; check the page source for `track.js`, `k_fac.php`, or form posts to raviral.com / sniperdz.com infrastructure (same template family). Pull WHOIS / GitHub repo owner if applicable. Step 2 (contain): Block the domain at the proxy. If users from your org reached the page, force credential reset for the impersonated brand's corporate SSO (if applicable) and revoke active sessions. Report to the hosting provider's abuse endpoint (GitHub, Netlify, Glitch all have rapid takedown). Step 3 (hunt): Extend the baseline window to 180d to surface long-tail Sniper Dz mirrors. Pivot the malicious URL into EmailEvents/EmailUrlInfo to find the delivery vector and the full recipient list.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

let LookbackDays = 7d;

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Europol Disrupts AudiA6 Crypto Laundering Service Used by Ransomware Gangs

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Authorities in Europe have disrupted AudiA6, a cryptocurrency laundering service used by ransomware gangs and cybercriminal networks. Europol, in a statement issued Thursday, said the dismantling of AudiA6 cut off a "key financial pipeline used to wash hundreds of millions in illicit profits." The service is estimated to have been used to launder more than €336 million (~$389 million) since the

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound or outbound email involving AudiA6 mule-recruitment domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS/network contact with AudiA6 money-mule registration domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DNS/network contact with AudiA6 money-mule registration domains AICommand & Control High
Detects endpoints resolving or connecting to the 19 email-infrastructure domains Europol linked to the AudiA6 crypto-laundering service. These domains were used to register fraudulent KYC accounts at cryptocurrency exchanges; a corporate device touching them indicates either an insider acting as a money mule, attacker reuse of corporate infrastructure for laundering, or recruitment communications reaching staff. Rationale: All 19 domains are taken verbatim from the Europol statement in the article body — they are confirmed by a primary law-enforcement source naming them as AudiA6-controlled infrastructure for mule account registration. No second-source web search was performed; the IOC list IS the primary-source bulletin. The domains are unusual second-level / vanity TLDs (.pictures, .top, .click, .agency, .express, .black, .email) so corporate baseline noise is near-zero, justifying alerting tier.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the Europol seizure page or VirusTotal pivot from a security workstation
  • Compliance / fraud team performing mule-account research against the published domain list
  • Researcher visiting the post-takedown Europol seizure banner now hosted on the seized domains
  • Honeypot / sinkhole resolution sweeps from a security tooling host enumerating IOC lists
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessAccountName !has_any ("soc","threatintel","fraud","compliance")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the resolving process and user — if InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser and the user belongs to security / fraud / compliance, check if they were actively reviewing the Europol bulletin (corroborate with browser history or ticket activity). Pull the device's user-context: insider risk score, finance/payments role, prior crypto-exchange traffic. Step 2 (contain): if the user is not a security researcher, isolate the device via Defender / Falcon Network Containment, suspend the AAD account, and block all 19 domains at the proxy/DNS layer pending review. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the device's last 30 days for outbound traffic to crypto-exchange APIs (binance, kraken, coinbase, kucoin), email to/from these same domains, and any KYC document uploads from the device; also sweep the org for any other host that resolved the same domain.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend HostLower = tolower(RemoteUrl)
| where HostLower has_any (AudiA6Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort

Inbound or outbound email involving AudiA6 mule-recruitment domains AIDelivery High
Detects email events where the sender or recipient domain matches one of the 19 AudiA6-controlled email domains identified by Europol. Article specifies these domains were used to register money-mule cryptocurrency exchange accounts using stolen identities and that Russian-speaking intermediaries were recruited via them — corporate email touching these domains indicates either mule-recruitment outreach or a staff member operating accounts on behalf of the laundering ring. Rationale: Article explicitly states AudiA6 'relied on both commercial email providers and email addresses linked to domains under their control to register money mule accounts' and recruited 'Russian-speaking intermediaries' via these channels — so inbound mail FROM these domains is recruitment outreach and outbound mail TO them is staff operating as mules. Sentinel KQL left empty because the provided Sentinel schema reference does not list a clean mailflow table (OfficeActivity covers admin operations, not full inbound metadata); operators on M365D-connected Sentinel tenants can re-use the Defender query verbatim against the imported EmailEvents table. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as none of those platforms ship M365 mailflow telemetry in the schemas referenced. Sigma skipped because Sigma's email logsource has no portable cross-vendor sender-domain selector matching this shape.
ATT&CKT1585.002 T1566
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Anti-fraud or threat-intel team mailing the AudiA6 domains for IOC validation / takedown coordination
  • A legitimate small SaaS that shared infrastructure on a generic vanity TLD (low risk given Europol seizure but possible for residual MX records on .email/.top domains)
  • Researcher subscribing a personal corporate mailbox to a blog newsletter that happens to send from one of the seized vanity domains pre-takedown
  • Quarantined / blocked spam that EmailEvents still records as a delivery attempt (DeliveryAction == Blocked) — analyst should treat these as a hit but lower severity
Suppression filter
| where not (RecipientEmailAddress has_any ("abuse@","soc@","threatintel@","fraud@") and EmailDirection == "Inbound")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the full message body via Threat Explorer / Content Search, check EmailDirection (Inbound = likely recruitment, Outbound = potential mule activity by the user). Examine sender display name, language (article notes Russian-speaking intermediaries), and any crypto-wallet addresses or exchange-platform links in the body. Step 2 (contain): if Outbound from an internal user, suspend the AAD account and seize the mailbox for forensics; if Inbound and delivered, soft-delete from all recipient mailboxes via Threat Explorer and add the sender domain to the tenant block-list. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the recipient/sender user — pull their 90-day SigninLogs for unusual geo, AAD app consents to crypto-wallet/exchange OAuth apps, and any DLP hits on outbound files containing identity documents (passport scans, utility bills) which are the KYC artifacts AudiA6 needed for mule registration.
let AudiA6Domains = dynamic(["designli.pictures","pheontx.eu","smplfy.in","sumato-soft.org","technobrains.dev","lett.email","trayo.app","deliverly.top","inboxly.top","postfast.eu","postino.click","inboxally.agency","mailora.eu","postify.email","quix.express","flowcomm.click","qube.black","deliverlett.com","lettermail.eu"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| extend SenderDom = tolower(SenderFromDomain), SenderMailDom = tolower(SenderMailFromDomain), RcptDom = tolower(tostring(split(RecipientEmailAddress, "@")[1]))
| where SenderDom in (AudiA6Domains) or SenderMailDom in (AudiA6Domains) or RcptDom in (AudiA6Domains)
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, EmailDirection, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, ThreatTypes, UrlCount, AttachmentCount
| order by Timestamp desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShinyHunters Exploits Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day (CVE-2026-35273) to Breach Universities

The Hacker NewsCISA KEV
2026-06-12 18 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The ShinyHunters extortion crew exploited an unpatched flaw in Oracle PeopleSoft to break into enterprise systems, steal data, and demand payment to keep it private. The campaign hit universities hardest. Google's Mandiant attributes it to the group it tracks as UNC6240, and dates the activity between May 27 and June 9. Oracle did not publish its advisory until June 10, so the bug was a

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MeshCentral Agent Masquerading as Microsoft Azure Binary · [LLM] Unexpected .jsp Webshell Drops Under PSEMHUB.war Application · [LLM] XMLDecoder Persistence via Modified envmetadata XML Files · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PeopleSoft Beacon to ShinyHunters C2 azurenetfiles.net · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ShinyHunters Ransom Marker File README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT · [LLM] SSH Fanout Lateral Movement Script ([host]_fanout.sh) on PeopleSoft Server · [LLM] zstd Compression of Bulk Data on PeopleSoft Host Pre-Exfiltration · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Oracle PeopleSoft CVE-2026-35273 Exploitation via PSEMHUB/hub POST AIExploitation Medium
Detects unauthenticated external POST requests to /PSEMHUB/hub or /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector — the exact endpoints Mandiant flagged as the CVE-2026-35273 exploitation surface for the UNC6240/ShinyHunters campaign against universities. Rationale: Article-specific URL paths (/PSEMHUB/hub and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector) named directly by Oracle/Mandiant as the CVE-2026-35273 exploitation endpoints. External-source filter keeps internal app-tier traffic out. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PSEMHUB heartbeat traffic from internal PeopleTools app servers reaching the hub via the public load balancer
  • Penetration tests or authorised vulnerability scans (Qualys/Nessus/Tenable) probing the PSEMHUB endpoint
  • Misconfigured internal admin browsing PSEMHUB from a corporate proxy egressing as a public IP
  • Health-check probes from external CDN/uptime monitors hitting the path
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<known_internal_admin_pool>") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Qualys","Nessus","Tenable","Nuclei")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full request body / Content-Length and User-Agent; check whether source IP appears in any threat-intel feed (especially the 142.11.200.186-190 staging block); confirm whether scStatus indicates a server processing the body or rejecting it. 2. Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter, remove external reachability of /PSEMHUB/* per Oracle guidance, and snapshot the PeopleSoft host for forensics before reboot (XMLDecoder persistence fires on restart). 3. Hunt: pivot to the same host for subsequent .jsp drops under PSEMHUB.war, new .xml writes under envmetadata/data/environment, outbound SMB/445, and connections to azurenetfiles.net within 24h.
// CVE-2026-35273 exploitation — Defender does not natively ship WebLogic / IIS access logs.
// If your PeopleSoft web tier ships W3CIIS logs into a custom table via Log Analytics agent, query that instead. The Sentinel rule below is the canonical implementation.
let StagingIPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/PSEMHUB/hub","/PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector","/PSEMHUB/")
| where scStatus between (200 .. 399)
| extend IsStagingIP = iif(cIP in (StagingIPs), "YES", "")
| extend IsRFC1918 = ipv4_is_private(cIP)
| where IsRFC1918 == false
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, cIP, IsStagingIP, csUserAgent, csBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
