PeopleSoft Beacon to ShinyHunters C2 azurenetfiles.net AICommand & Control Medium
Detects DNS or network egress to azurenetfiles.net — the UNC6240/ShinyHunters C2 domain typosquatting Azure NetApp Files and called home by the MeshCentral agents staged on victim PeopleSoft hosts. Rationale: azurenetfiles.net is the campaign-specific C2 domain Mandiant attributed to UNC6240, and the 142.11.200.186-190/108.174.202.99/176.120.22.24 IPs were the Python SimpleHTTP staging servers exposed by @nahamike01. Both indicators corroborated in vendor write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/EDR detonation of a sample that includes the domain (filter on internal sandbox CIDR)
  • Researcher / threat-intel analyst workstation manually pivoting on the IOC
  • Passive DNS resolver in security stack pre-resolving the IOC for blocklists
  • DNS sinkhole already redirecting the domain — log entry without real exfiltration
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandbox.exe","cuckoo.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "SOC-RESEARCH-"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the initiating process and full command line; confirm whether the host is a PeopleSoft application/web tier node or a downstream lateral-movement target; pull memory / process listing before reboot. 2. Contain: isolate the device from network, block azurenetfiles.net + all 7 staging IPs at perimeter and internal DNS, kill any MeshCentral agent process disguised as an Azure-named binary (see related UC). 3. Hunt: search the prior 30d for any host that resolved the domain, any user account that authenticated from the host during the beacon window, presence of /tmp/<victim>_fanout.sh, README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT marker files, and zstd archive creation events.

union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has C2Domain or RemoteIP in (StagingIPs)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where RemoteUrl has C2Domain
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc

union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents

(CommonSecurityLog

  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceAction),
(ImDnsActivity

MeshCentral Agent Masquerading as Microsoft Azure Binary AIInstallation Medium
Detects processes named to look like Microsoft Azure binaries but actually MeshCentral remote-management agents deployed by UNC6240. Mandiant identified custom MeshCentral builds disguised as Azure naming on staging servers. Rationale: Article: 'custom MeshCentral remote-management agents disguised as Microsoft Azure binaries'. Detection pairs a name pattern (azure/netapp/netfiles) with location-mismatch + non-Microsoft signer + MeshCentral install switches to keep FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/ • https://github.com/Ylianst/MeshCentral
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Microsoft Azure CLI / Azure agent installs from non-standard MSI paths (rare on PeopleSoft hosts)
  • Internal IT-built `AzureMonitor` repackaged installer dropping under ProgramData
  • Developer machines with `azure-*-cli.exe` artifacts under user profile build dirs
  • Azure DevOps self-hosted agents shipping `Agent.Listener.exe` (different name but adjacent space)
Suppression filter
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "Microsoft Corporation" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Azure"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull SHA256 and check against VirusTotal / abuse.ch for known MeshAgent builds; inspect command line for --meshServiceName / agentid arguments; map the process tree to identify how the binary landed. 2. Contain: isolate host, kill the process tree, remove the Service registration (Get-Service / sc.exe), capture the binary for IR triage, and rotate credentials of any user who interactively logged into the host since first execution. 3. Hunt: pivot on SHA256 across the fleet, then look for the file landing via SCP/SFTP from any of the 7 staging IPs in the prior 30d, and for outbound to azurenetfiles.net.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(azure|netapp|netfiles|meshagent).*\.(exe|bin|elf)?$"
| where not(FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Microsoft Azure", @"\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Azure", @"\WindowsApps\", @"\ProgramData\Microsoft\Azure"))
| where not(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Microsoft Corporation")
| extend SuspiciousMesh = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--meshServiceName","meshcentral","--installAsService","agentid","MeshAgent")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, SuspiciousMesh, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(azure|netapp|netfiles|meshagent).*\.(exe|bin|elf)?$"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Program Files\Microsoft Azure\", @"\WindowsApps\"))
| where not(ActingProcessFileCompany has "Microsoft Corporation")
| extend SuspiciousMesh = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--meshServiceName","meshcentral","--installAsService","MeshAgent")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessFileDescription, SHA256, ParentProcessName, SuspiciousMesh
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ShinyHunters Ransom Marker File README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the creation of the literal marker filename UNC6240's fanout script drops into PeopleSoft directories after a successful lateral-movement spray. The filename string is unique to this campaign. Rationale: Verbatim article string: 'drops a marker file named README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT into PeopleSoft directories'. The filename is unique enough to act as a definitive trip-wire. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence
ATT&CKT1485 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel team copying the IOC into a docs folder for awareness
  • Backup process replicating a previously-compromised host's tree into a backup vault
  • SIEM rule testing / purple-team simulation deliberately writing the file
  • Email gateway extraction of an inbound article-attachment containing the string
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the writing process and parent — the fanout script (.sh) is the expected dropper; identify if this is the originating host or a fanout target. 2. Contain: isolate host immediately, capture memory + disk, kill all live SSH sessions originating from PeopleSoft context, and rotate every credential present in the host's /etc/hosts spray scope. 3. Hunt: for the same host trace the previous 7d for inbound SSH from RFC1918 / from the 142.11.200.186-190 staging range, presence of /tmp/<host>_fanout.sh, zstd archive creation, and outbound SSH on 22 to internet IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let MarkerName = "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT";
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetFileName =~ MarkerName
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType),
(Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where SyslogMessage has MarkerName
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unexpected .jsp Webshell Drops Under PSEMHUB.war Application AIInstallation High
Detects creation of .jsp files under the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub web application directory or odd folder names (logs, persistantstorage, scratchpad) — Oracle/Mandiant guidance flags these as post-exploitation webshell indicators. Rationale: Verbatim Oracle/Mandiant guidance from article: 'Unexpected .jsp files under the PSEMHUB.war web application directory, or odd folders named logs, persistantstorage, or scratchpad under the PSEMHUB paths.' Mis-spelt 'persistantstorage' is the attacker's literal artifact name. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Oracle-provided PeopleTools patch (CPU/PSU) legitimately writing under PSEMHUB during a documented maintenance window
  • Internal developer adding a custom integration JSP for testing (correlate with change-control)
  • Backup restore replacing the war directory contents from a known-good snapshot
  • Antivirus quarantine action moving a flagged JSP within the directory tree
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("<change_control_peoplesoft_admin>") and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "OPatch"
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the .jsp contents, check for hex-encoded / base64 payloads, identify the writing process (typically WebLogic JVM under peoplesoft user), correlate against the W3CIIS POST detection within the previous 30 min. 2. Contain: isolate the host, remove the .jsp drop and the odd folders, snapshot disk for forensics (XMLDecoder triggers on restart so do not reboot before disk image), revoke the WebLogic service account credentials. 3. Hunt: search every PeopleSoft host for the same TargetFileName SHA256, related .xml writes under envmetadata/data/environment, and outbound to azurenetfiles.net.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("PSEMHUB.war","/PSEMHUB/","\\PSEMHUB\\")
| where FileName endswith ".jsp"
   or FolderPath has_any ("/persistantstorage/","\\persistantstorage\\","/scratchpad/","\\scratchpad\\","/logs/","\\logs\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileWritten")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("PSEMHUB.war","/PSEMHUB/",@"\PSEMHUB\")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "jsp"
   or TargetFilePath has_any ("persistantstorage","scratchpad")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileExtension, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XMLDecoder Persistence via Modified envmetadata XML Files AIInstallation High
Detects modification or creation of .xml files under the PeopleSoft envmetadata/data/environment directory — Oracle's mitigation guidance specifically calls out this path as the XMLDecoder persistence vector that fires on next PeopleSoft restart. Rationale: Verbatim from article: 'Recently changed .xml files under the web doc root's envmetadata/data/environment, which can be abused for XMLDecoder persistence that fires on the next restart.' This is the specific persistence pathway named in vendor guidance. Cross-checked against: • https://www.oracle.com/security-alerts/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/
ATT&CKT1505 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned PeopleTools environment configuration import or patch maintenance window
  • Database refresh / refresh-from-prod cycle that legitimately rewrites environment metadata
  • Replication of envmetadata between an HA pair
  • Backup verification job touching mtime without actual content change
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("<peoplesoft_admin_pool>") and ActingProcessName !has_any ("OPatch","PSADMIN","PSADMIN.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: diff the newly-written XML against the last known-good copy (look for java.beans.XMLDecoder class invocations, ProcessBuilder, Runtime.exec, hex/base64 blobs); identify the writing process — should normally be a PeopleTools admin user or the PSEMHUB JVM, not a webserver request handler. 2. Contain: restore the XML from a verified backup BEFORE the next PeopleSoft service restart, then patch per Oracle My Oracle Support document and lock down /PSEMHUB/*. 3. Hunt: cross-reference the writing process tree to W3CIISLog POSTs to /PSEMHUB/hub in the same window, and pivot to other envmetadata directories on the same host for similar writes.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("envmetadata/data/environment","envmetadata\\data\\environment")
| where FileName endswith ".xml"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileWritten")
| where TargetFilePath has "envmetadata/data/environment" or TargetFilePath has @"envmetadata\data\environment"
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "xml"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound SMB/445 from PeopleSoft Hosts to Internet (NetNTLM Capture) AIExploitation High
Detects outbound SMB on TCP/445 from PeopleSoft application servers to external IP addresses — Oracle/Mandiant note the CVE-2026-35273 exploit chain may coerce the server to authenticate outbound, leaking machine-account NetNTLMv2 hashes. Rationale: Verbatim from article: 'Outbound SMB traffic on port 445 from PeopleSoft hosts to external destinations, which the exploit chain may use to capture machine-account NetNTLM hashes.' Outbound /445/Public from a PeopleSoft host is highly anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1187/
ATT&CKT1187 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DR replication leveraging SMB over routed public infrastructure to an off-site DR location
  • Misconfigured monitoring tool path that includes a public reachability test on 445
  • Cloud-backed file share (Azure Files / FSx) over public endpoint
  • Legacy backup-to-cloud agent
  • Site-to-site VPN failover routing SMB over a public IP briefly during cutover
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr !in (dynamic(["<sanctioned_dr_smb_ip_1>","<sanctioned_dr_smb_ip_2>"]))
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture full netflow including destination IP/AS/reverse DNS; confirm destination is not a sanctioned Azure Files / DR endpoint; pull the WebLogic / Java process command line that owned the socket. 2. Contain: block outbound 445 from the PeopleSoft subnet at perimeter (best practice regardless), rotate the host's machine account secret, and disable NTLM authentication via group policy where feasible. 3. Hunt: cross-reference timestamp with W3CIISLog POSTs to /PSEMHUB/hub or /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector; search domain controllers for subsequent NTLM relay-style authentications using the leaked machine account credential.
let PeopleSoftHosts = dynamic(["<peoplesoft-app-01>","<peoplesoft-app-02>","<peoplesoft-web-01>"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where DeviceName in~ (PeopleSoftHosts) or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("PSAPPSRV","PSPRCSRV","PSEMAGENT","weblogic","java")
| where RemotePort == 445
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let PeopleSoftHosts = dynamic(["<peoplesoft-app-01>","<peoplesoft-app-02>","<peoplesoft-web-01>"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstPortNumber == 445
| where DvcHostname in~ (PeopleSoftHosts) or SrcHostname in~ (PeopleSoftHosts)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes, EventResult, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SSH Fanout Lateral Movement Script ([host]_fanout.sh) on PeopleSoft Server AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation or execution of UNC6240's lateral-movement script — named [victim]_fanout.sh — which sprays a hardcoded SSH credential list against hosts harvested from /etc/hosts on the compromised PeopleSoft server. Rationale: Verbatim from article: 'The script, named [victim]_fanout.sh, spreads over SSH by spraying a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords against internal hosts pulled from /etc/hosts'. Naming convention <victim>_fanout.sh + parsing /etc/hosts + sshpass combo is unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/004/
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1110.003 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned automation tool (Ansible, Rundeck, Jenkins) executing SSH fanout for batch admin
  • Internal red team / pentest engagement explicitly authorised to use sshpass
  • Custom DR runbook with similarly-named cluster-fanout.sh script
  • Backup-orchestration script reading /etc/hosts to build a target list
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("ansible","jenkins","rundeck") and ActingProcessCommandLine !has "#PURPLE-TEAM"
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the .sh file contents, identify the hardcoded credential list and the target host set parsed from /etc/hosts; confirm which downstream hosts were reached via the audit log. 2. Contain: kill the script process tree, revoke every credential present in the hardcoded list across the directory, isolate the source host, and quarantine all confirmed-reached downstream hosts pending forensics. 3. Hunt: for each target host pulled from /etc/hosts on the source, look for new SSH successful logons in the script execution window, presence of the README marker file, zstd archive creation, and outbound SSH-on-22 to the public mirror of the ShinyHunters leak site.
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*_fanout\.sh$"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "_fanout.sh" or FileName == "sshpass"
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "/etc/hosts" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ssh ","scp ","sshpass"))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^.*_fanout\.sh$"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "_fanout.sh" or ActingProcessName endswith "sshpass"
     or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "/etc/hosts" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ssh ","sshpass","scp "))
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine),
(Syslog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)_fanout\.sh"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

zstd Compression of Bulk Data on PeopleSoft Host Pre-Exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects use of zstd to compress large archives on a PeopleSoft host immediately followed by outbound SSH/SCP — Mandiant's command-history triage showed UNC6240 used 'zstd' for data compression and then SSH'd the archive to the ShinyHunters leak-site mirror. Rationale: Verbatim from article: 'The command history shows the data compressed with zstd and an outbound SSH connection to the server hosting the public mirror of the ShinyHunters leak site.' Pairing zstd with PeopleSoft application paths keeps FPs from legitimate log-rotation jobs low. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1560/001/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned PeopleSoft backup script using zstd for log/data archive
  • Database snapshot export pipeline ending in zstd compression
  • Engineering team using zstd to compress troubleshooting captures
  • Custom PeopleTools migration tool packaging envmetadata for an upgrade
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in~ ("<peoplesoft_backup_svc>","backup","oracle") and ParentProcessName !has_any ("cron","systemd","backup")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the calling shell + parent process, capture the resulting archive path/size, check whether the archive was opened over an SSH/SCP session in the same window. 2. Contain: terminate the process, prevent file egress (quarantine archive), block outbound SSH to non-corporate IPs from PeopleSoft subnet at perimeter, snapshot the host. 3. Hunt: pivot to outbound SSH (port 22) destinations from the same host in the same window, cross-reference against the ShinyHunters public-mirror infrastructure list, and search for parallel zstd runs across the PeopleSoft fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "zstd" or ProcessCommandLine has_any (" zstd ","zstd --","|zstd ")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PS_HOME","peoplesoft","envmetadata","PS_APP_HOME",".tar","-19","--ultra")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "zstd" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (" zstd ","zstd --","|zstd ")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PS_HOME","peoplesoft","envmetadata","PS_APP_HOME",".tar","-19","--ultra")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort

ImNetworkSession

            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber

| order by ConnCount desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35273")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High

DeviceProcessEvents

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Dropper filename pattern: MD5-prefixed Exe.exe and VID001.exe lure
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — A tale of two eras
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos weekly top-prevalent malware hash execution (Coinminer/Injector/Miner Dropper) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Talos weekly top-prevalent malware hash execution (Coinminer/Injector/Miner Dropper) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution or write of the four SHA256/MD5 IOCs Talos flagged this week as the most prevalent files in their telemetry: Win.Worm.Coinminer::1201 (VID001.exe), W32.Injector:Gen.21ie.1201, and two Win.Dropper.Miner::95.sbx.tg samples. High-fidelity because the hashes are vendor-published prevalent-malware IOCs from the same week as the article. Rationale: Hashes and MD5s are lifted verbatim from Talos's 'Most prevalent malware files from Talos telemetry over the past week' block in the article body. The Talos File Reputation URLs published alongside each hash (talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=<hash>) serve as the second-source vendor-confirmed corroboration — each is a permanent vendor advisory page. Cross-checked against: • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1496 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst sandbox detonating the same sample on a corp-imaged VM for triage
  • Red-team / purple-team exercise dropping known-IOC samples to validate detection coverage
  • SOC-deployed canary file with an intentionally-matched hash used to verify ingestion
  • Reverse-engineering lab host where these binaries are reviewed under controlled conditions
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "SANDBOX-" and DeviceName !startswith "RE-LAB-" and DeviceName !startswith "REDTEAM-"
Response runbook
1. Triage: open the alert, confirm the host is not in the sandbox / RE / red-team VLAN, and pull the full process tree + parent for the matching SHA256/MD5. Check Talos File Reputation URL for the specific verdict tier. 2. Contain: isolate the device via MDE Live Response (or equivalent), quarantine the file by hash across the fleet, suspend the user account if interactive logon evidence is present. 3. Hunt: pivot on parent process / dropper folder path / write-source URL — look for siblings dropped by the same parent, sweep all endpoints for the four hashes + MD5s in this UC across the prior 30 days, and check for outbound connections from the parent process to mining pools or C2.
let TalosWeeklyHashes_SHA256 = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f"]);
let TalosWeeklyHashes_MD5 = dynamic(["2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where SHA256 in~ (TalosWeeklyHashes_SHA256) or MD5 in~ (TalosWeeklyHashes_MD5)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="DeviceProcessEvents";
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
    | where SHA256 in~ (TalosWeeklyHashes_SHA256) or MD5 in~ (TalosWeeklyHashes_MD5)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="DeviceFileEvents";
union ProcHits, FileHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let TalosWeeklyHashes_SHA256 = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f"]);
let TalosWeeklyHashes_MD5 = dynamic(["2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
let ProcHits = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where SHA256 in~ (TalosWeeklyHashes_SHA256) or MD5 in~ (TalosWeeklyHashes_MD5)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5, ParentProcessName, Source="ImProcessCreate";
let FileHits = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (TalosWeeklyHashes_SHA256) or TargetFileMD5 in~ (TalosWeeklyHashes_MD5)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256, MD5=TargetFileMD5, ParentProcessName="", Source="ImFileEvent";
union ProcHits, FileHits
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_sha256 in ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f") OR Processes.process_hash in ("2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_sha256 Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | append [| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_hash in ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_sha256 in ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f") OR Processes.process_hash in ("2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f","aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9","7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376","38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_sha256 Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_hash in ("9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507","96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974","a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91","9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`]
Dropper filename pattern: MD5-prefixed Exe.exe and VID001.exe lure AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the distinctive dropper naming convention Talos surfaced this week — files of shape `<32-hex-md5>_<NN>_Exe.exe` (e.g. d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_62_Exe.exe and _63_Exe.exe) and the social-engineering lure filename VID001.exe (video-impersonation .exe). Useful as a hash-independent catch when the campaign repacks but keeps its naming template. Rationale: Filenames `VID001.exe`, `d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_63_Exe.exe`, and `d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_62_Exe.exe` are taken verbatim from the article's prevalent-malware block. The shared `d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_*_Exe.exe` structure across two distinct hashes shows a templated dropper convention worth hunting on independent of the specific binary hash — repack-resistant. Cross-checked against: • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974 • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal build pipeline that hashes artefacts and appends a sequence index (uncommon naming convention but possible)
  • Malware analyst preserving original sample filenames on a triage host
  • Forensic tooling that hashes files and renames evidence using a similar template
  • Legitimate video-converter or video-editor temp file accidentally named VID001.exe
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "BUILD-" and DeviceName !startswith "SANDBOX-" and DeviceName !startswith "RE-LAB-" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\Cisco\AMP"
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the host is not a build runner / RE / forensics lab and capture full process/file lineage including FileOriginUrl + FileOriginReferrerUrl (Defender) — where did the file land from? 2. Contain: quarantine the file (and its MD5-prefix hash if observed), isolate the device, capture memory if process is still running. 3. Hunt: pivot on the exact 32-hex MD5 prefix observed in the filename — query other endpoints for the same prefix with different `_NN_Exe.exe` suffixes (the campaign appears to sequence samples). Pull network telemetry from the dropper process for mining-pool indicators or staging URLs.
let DropperFileEvents = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
    | where FileName =~ "VID001.exe"
        or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$"
    | extend MD5PrefixFromName = extract(@"(?i)^([0-9a-f]{32})_\d+_Exe\.exe$", 1, FileName)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, MD5PrefixFromName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, Source="DeviceFileEvents";
let DropperProcEvents = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName =~ "VID001.exe"
        or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$"
    | extend MD5PrefixFromName = extract(@"(?i)^([0-9a-f]{32})_\d+_Exe\.exe$", 1, FileName)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, MD5PrefixFromName, ActionType="ProcessCreated", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileOriginUrl="", FileOriginReferrerUrl="", Source="DeviceProcessEvents";
union DropperFileEvents, DropperProcEvents
| order by Timestamp desc
let DropperFiles = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileName =~ "VID001.exe"
        or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$"
    | extend MD5PrefixFromName = extract(@"(?i)^([0-9a-f]{32})_\d+_Exe\.exe$", 1, TargetFileName)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, FileName=TargetFileName, FilePath=TargetFilePath, SHA256=TargetFileSHA256, MD5=TargetFileMD5, MD5PrefixFromName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImFileEvent";
let DropperProcs = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(?:^|[\\/])VID001\.exe$"
        or ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)[\\/][0-9a-f]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$"
    | extend FileName = tostring(split(ActingProcessName, @"\")[-1])
    | extend MD5PrefixFromName = extract(@"(?i)^([0-9a-f]{32})_\d+_Exe\.exe$", 1, FileName)
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, FileName, FilePath=ActingProcessName, SHA256, MD5, MD5PrefixFromName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImProcessCreate";
union DropperFiles, DropperProcs
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Talos Weekly Dropper Filename Pattern (VID001.exe / MD5-prefixed Exe.exe)
id: 2f1a8c4e-6d9b-4e3a-bc12-5a7d8f4c1e9b
description: Detects the distinctive dropper naming template Talos observed in the week of 2026-06-11 — VID001.exe video-lure and files named `<32-hex-md5>_<NN>_Exe.exe` (e.g. d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_62_Exe.exe). Hash-independent — survives repack.
references:
    - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/a-tale-of-two-eras/
author: Talos UC pipeline
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.t1036.005
    - attack.t1105
logsource:
    category: file_event
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_vid:
        TargetFilename|endswith: '\VID001.exe'
    selection_pattern:
        TargetFilename|re: '(?i)\\[0-9a-f]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$'
    condition: selection_vid or selection_pattern
falsepositives:
    - Internal automation that hashes-then-names build artefacts using a similar template (rare — confirm with build engineering)
    - Malware analyst saving samples with original-name preserved
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:(1 OR 11) (@TargetFilename:(*\\VID001.exe OR *\\vid001.exe) OR @Image:(*\\VID001.exe OR *\\vid001.exe) OR @TargetFilename:*_Exe.exe OR @Image:*_Exe.exe)
#event_simpleName=/^(ProcessRollup2|FileWritten)$/
| ImageFileName=/[\\/]VID001\.exe$/i OR TargetFileName=/[\\/]VID001\.exe$/i OR ImageFileName=/[\\/][0-9a-f]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$/i OR TargetFileName=/[\\/][0-9a-f]{32}_\d+_Exe\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, #event_simpleName, ImageFileName, TargetFileName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="VID001.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_*_Exe.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | rex field=file_name "^(?<md5_prefix>[0-9a-f]{32})_(?<seq>\d+)_Exe\.exe$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | append [| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="VID001.exe" OR Processes.process_name="d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_*_Exe.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="VID001.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_*_Exe.exe") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | rex field=file_name "^(?<md5_prefix>[0-9a-f]{32})_(?<seq>\d+)_Exe\.exe$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="VID001.exe" OR Processes.process_name="d4aa3e7010220ad1b458fac17039c274_*_Exe.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |

    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'

            - '\svchost.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "a31f222fc283227f5e7988d1ad9c0aecd66d58bb7b4d8518ae23e110308dbf91", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9", "7bdbd180c081fa63ca94f9c22c457376", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Attacks Trick OpenClaw AI Agent Into Running Code and Leaking Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-06-11 14 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Two security teams have shown, in separate research published this week, that OpenClaw, the popular self-hosted AI agent, can be driven to run attacker-controlled code or hand over sensitive data through ordinary-looking inputs. Imperva buried instructions inside shared contacts, vCards, and location pins that the agent executed without the victim ever seeing them. Varonis built a test agent on

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Outdated OpenClaw AI agent (<2026.4.23) — vulnerable to vCard/contact prompt inj
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell / script interpreter (code execution from agent context) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent process connecting to Imperva PoC domain imperva_artifactory.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OpenClaw / Pinchy agent forwarding credential-shaped strings to external mailbox · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
OpenClaw agent process connecting to Imperva PoC domain imperva_artifactory.com AICommand & Control High
Detects any host where the OpenClaw AI agent (or any process) reaches out to imperva_artifactory.com, the domain Imperva used in their disclosure to host the payload script their hidden vCard/contact prompt injection downloaded and executed. Re-use of this exact host in the wild would be a strong PoC-mimicry / copycat-attack signal. Rationale: imperva_artifactory.com is the only concrete IOC in the article body (pre-extracted IOC list). It is Imperva's PoC payload-host domain used in the vCard/contact prompt-injection demo; any production traffic to it is either copycat exploitation or a researcher rerunning the PoC inside the estate. Cross-checked: domain string appears verbatim in the article and the IOC extraction header.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red team replaying the Imperva PoC for tabletop / training
  • Security researcher on corporate net reading the Imperva blog and following the link
  • Sandbox / EDR detonating a sample copied from the disclosure into a lab segment
  • Web proxy URL-categorization service scanning the domain proactively
  • Threat-intel platform automatically validating the IOC by resolving it
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName has_any ("explorer.exe","outlook.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) and confirm whether the source host is running OpenClaw or another AI-agent runtime; check user agent and parent chain for evidence of script download (curl/wget/bash -c). Step 2 — Contain: block imperva_artifactory.com at the egress proxy / DNS RPZ, isolate the host if any file write or child-process spawn followed the connection, rotate any cloud credentials reachable from the agent's mailbox/secret store. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same agent process across other hosts for any other low-reputation domain in the same 24h window; review OpenClaw `memory` store contents for the injected instruction (Imperva flagged memory-on as the amplifier); check inbound WhatsApp / vCard / shared-location feeds the agent ingested in the hour before the connect.
let ImpervaPoC = dynamic(["imperva_artifactory.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (ImpervaPoC) or tostring(AdditionalFields) has "imperva_artifactory"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let ImpervaPoC = dynamic(["imperva_artifactory.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where RequestURL has_any (ImpervaPoC) or DestinationHostName has_any (ImpervaPoC)
   | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, ProcessName=SourceProcessName, DeviceProduct),
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has_any (ImpervaPoC)
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType),
  (ImWebSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Url has_any (ImpervaPoC) or HttpHostName has_any (ImpervaPoC)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpHostName, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell / script interpreter (code execution from agent context) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the OpenClaw agent process (python/node runtime hosting OpenClaw) spawning a shell or script interpreter as a child — the exact behaviour Imperva proved by getting Gemini 3.1 Pro inside OpenClaw to download and run a remote script. Targets the article's central claim that the agent can be driven to run attacker-controlled code from a hidden contact/vCard payload. Rationale: Article: 'the hidden text told the agent to download and run a script from a server the researchers controlled. It did.' That is parent=agent → child=download tool / shell. Pivots on agent-process names ('openclaw', 'pinchy' — Pinchy is the Varonis-built OpenClaw agent named in the article) parent → standard LOLBin / interpreter children. Sigma covers the single-event shape.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.004 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OpenClaw legitimately invoking a Python helper subprocess as part of a curated tool (e.g. data-analysis plugin)
  • Developer running OpenClaw in dev mode and shelling out to test scripts
  • OpenClaw auto-update routine invoking curl/wget to fetch an update manifest
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting OpenClaw with a wrapping bash/cmd parent
  • Health-check probe that execs `python --version` from the agent container
Suppression filter
and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--version","-V","--help") and ChildCmd !has "http")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the child cmdline and check whether the invocation pattern matches a documented OpenClaw plugin or is unsanctioned (e.g. `curl http... | bash`, `powershell -nop -enc ...`); pull the agent's recent message ingest (WhatsApp shared contacts, vCards, location pins) for the 30 min before the spawn — Imperva's payload is the contact `name` field. Step 2 — Contain: kill the child, suspend the OpenClaw agent process, snapshot memory, and disable network egress for the host until reviewed; rotate any tokens the agent has access to. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the SHA256 of the child binary across the estate; search for the same parent→child shape on other agent hosts; verify OpenClaw is at 2026.4.23 or later (the Imperva fix); review whether memory is enabled on the agent — Imperva specifically warned poisoned memory amplifies one injection across many agents.
let AgentParents = dynamic(["openclaw","openclaw.exe","openclaw-agent","pinchy"]);
let RiskyChildren = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","node.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any (AgentParents)
      or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (AgentParents)
      or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "openclaw"
| where FileName in~ (RiskyChildren)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage=FolderPath,
          ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let AgentParents = dynamic(["openclaw","openclaw.exe","openclaw-agent","pinchy"]);
let RiskyChildren = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","node.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where EventID == 4688
   | where ParentProcessName has_any (AgentParents)
   | extend ChildName = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,'\\')[-1]))
   | where ChildName in~ (RiskyChildren)
   | where AccountName !endswith "$"
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine),
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where ParentProcessName has_any (AgentParents)
   | where TargetProcessName has_any (RiskyChildren)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: OpenClaw AI Agent Spawning Shell or Interpreter
id: 8e2c4d31-5f7a-4c9b-b1d8-3a9e7f6c2d54
description: Detects the OpenClaw AI agent runtime spawning a shell, scripting host, or download tool as a child process — the post-prompt-injection RCE shape demonstrated by Imperva (Jun 2026) where a hidden vCard instruction caused OpenClaw to download and execute a remote script.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-attacks-trick-openclaw-ai-agent.html
author: Detection Pipeline
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - 'openclaw'
      - 'pinchy'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\bash.exe'
      - '\sh'
      - '\wsl.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security OR linux.auditd) AND @EventID:(1 OR 4688) AND (@ParentImage:(*\\openclaw* OR *\\OpenClaw* OR *\\pinchy*) OR @ParentCommandLine:(*openclaw* OR *OpenClaw* OR *pinchy*) OR @process.parent.name:(openclaw* OR OpenClaw* OR pinchy*)) AND (@Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\bash.exe OR *\\sh OR *\\python.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\certutil.exe) OR @process.name:(cmd.exe OR powershell.exe OR bash OR sh OR python OR node OR curl OR wget OR certutil.exe))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/openclaw|pinchy/i OR ParentImageFileName=/openclaw|pinchy/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|bash|sh|wsl|python|pythonw|node|curl|wget|certutil|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i OR ImageFileName=/\/(bash|sh|python3?|node|curl|wget)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_cmd values(Processes.process) as child_cmd values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="openclaw*" OR Processes.parent_process="*openclaw*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\openclaw\\*") (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","python.exe","node.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe")) by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
OpenClaw / Pinchy agent forwarding credential-shaped strings to external mailbox AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects an OpenClaw-driven mailbox sending out a message whose body contains credential-shaped strings (AWS access keys, SSH private keys, JDBC connection strings) to an external recipient — the exact agent-phishing outcome Varonis reproduced where a single plain email talked Pinchy into forwarding mock AWS IAM keys, DB connection strings and SSH credentials in plaintext. Rationale: Article: Pinchy 'forwarded mock AWS IAM access keys, database connection strings, and SSH credentials in plaintext' to a fake Dan asking for staging access. Detection chains the agent-named sender (openclaw / pinchy) with classic credential markers (AWS AKIA/ASIA prefix, OpenSSH/RSA PEM headers, JDBC connection strings) being sent to an external recipient. Sigma omitted: this is a multi-table join (Email + CloudApp) and would not collapse into one selection.
ATT&CKT1567 T1114.003 T1552.001
Data sourcesEmail.Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT ticket reply from an automation account quoting redacted credential format examples
  • Security training email containing fake-looking AWS keys for awareness exercise
  • Pinchy / OpenClaw running its sanctioned 'rotate key' workflow that legitimately mails new credentials to an internal vault address (intra-org)
  • Developer onboarding email shipping a vault URL + redacted snippet to a contractor (external but expected)
  • DLP product mirroring a quarantined message back to a SOC mailbox for review
Suppression filter
and not (Subject has_any ("[TEST]","[DRILL]","[TRAINING]") and RecipientEmailAddress endswith "@yourcorp.com")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full message body via Threat Explorer / Vault, confirm the credentials are LIVE (not example strings), and map the inbound trigger — Varonis showed both attack pretexts (urgency 'Dan from incident' and routine 'weekly customer export'); search the agent's inbox for the trigger message in the 2h window before send. Step 2 — Contain: recall / soft-delete the outbound mail, rotate every credential disclosed (AWS keys, SSH, DB strings), block the recipient domain, and pause the agent's outbound-mail connector until policy is tightened — Varonis' recommended control is a first-time-recipient gate. Step 3 — Hunt: search OfficeActivity / Gmail audit for the same sender→external pattern with any credential marker over 30 days; review whether the OpenClaw instruction file enforces sender verification (Varonis: 'the rule existed. Urgency beat it once, routine beat it the second time.'); check Defender for Cloud Apps for the agent's connector trust level matches mailbox 
let AgentSenders = dynamic(["openclaw","pinchy"]);
let CredentialMarkers = dynamic(["AKIA","ASIA","aws_secret_access_key","BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY","BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY","BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY","jdbc:mysql","jdbc:postgresql","mongodb+srv","Server=","Data Source=","PRIVATE_KEY"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection in ("Outbound","Intra-org")
| where SenderDisplayName has_any (AgentSenders)

| where Subject has_any (CredentialMarkers)

| where RecipientEmailAddress !endswith "@yourcorp.com"
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderDisplayName, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, ThreatTypes, NetworkMessageId, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let AgentSenders = dynamic(["openclaw","pinchy"]);
let CredentialMarkers = dynamic(["AKIA","ASIA","aws_secret_access_key","BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY","BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY","jdbc:mysql","jdbc:postgresql","mongodb+srv","Server=","Data Source=","PRIVATE_KEY"]);
OfficeActivity

| where Operation in ("Send","SendAs","SendOnBehalf","Create")
| where UserId has_any (AgentSenders) or ClientInfoString has_any (AgentSenders)

source:(google_workspace OR gmail OR office365 OR microsoft365) AND (@evt.name:(*send* OR *Send* OR mail.send) OR @event.action:send) AND (@actor.user.email:*openclaw* OR @actor.user.email:*pinchy* OR @from:*openclaw* OR @from:*pinchy* OR @user.name:(openclaw* OR pinchy*)) AND (@email.subject:(*AKIA* OR *aws_secret* OR *PRIVATE\ KEY* OR *jdbc\:* OR *mongodb*) OR @email.body:(*AKIA* OR *BEGIN\ OPENSSH\ PRIVATE\ KEY* OR *BEGIN\ RSA\ PRIVATE\ KEY* OR *aws_secret_access_key* OR *jdbc\:mysql* OR *mongodb+srv*)) AND -@to:*@yourcorp.com
