File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-06-11 15 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

npm v12 makes install scripts opt-in by default, closing the install-time execution path behind a year of npm supply chain worms from Nx to Red Hat. Category: News

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] npm install with --ignore-scripts override bypassing v12 postinstall protection
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — npm v12 delivers one of the biggest security improvements in years
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm/node spawning shell or downloader during package install (postinstall hook abuse) · [LLM] Bun runtime dropped or executed by node/npm child process (Shai-Hulud signature) · [LLM] Known npm supply-chain malware hash observed on disk or in execution · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network connection to npm supply-chain attack IOCs (sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73 / webhook.site) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] TruffleHog credential scanner executed from node/npm context · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
npm/node spawning shell or downloader during package install (postinstall hook abuse) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the core threat the article describes: npm/node/yarn/pnpm spawning a shell, downloader LOLBin, or known supply-chain tool (bun, trufflehog) as a child during `npm install`. This is the execution shape used by Nx s1ngularity's telemetry.js, Shai-Hulud, axios hijack, and Mini Shai-Hulud postinstall/preinstall hooks. Rationale: Anchors on the article's central thesis: postinstall/preinstall hooks run `npm install` lifecycle scripts as arbitrary code. Nx s1ngularity (telemetry.js), Shai-Hulud (Bun + TruffleHog), axios hijack (RAT), and Mini Shai-Hulud all manifest as node/npm parent → shell/downloader child. The child list specifically includes `bun.exe` and `trufflehog.exe` because the article names both as Shai-Hulud's runtime/tooling.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1195.002 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp legitimately spawning cmd.exe to invoke MSVC for native module builds (sqlite3, bcrypt, sharp)
  • electron-builder spawning powershell.exe for Authenticode code-signing during release builds
  • husky git hooks invoking sh/bash via npm scripts (lint-staged, commitlint)
  • Nx/Lerna monorepo orchestrators spawning shells to fan tasks across packages
  • CI runners (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab) where npm scripts legitimately shell out (`npm run build` → shell)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","electron-builder","husky","lint-staged") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("jenkins.exe","runner.exe","Agent.Worker.exe","actions-runner.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree (grandparent of npm, the package being installed, and post-child activity). Check `InitiatingProcessCommandLine` for `npm install <package>@<version>` to identify which package triggered. Look up the package on npm registry — was a new version published in the last 7 days? 2) Contain: if the package is unknown or recently re-published, isolate the host via MDE/EDR, kill the child chain, and revoke any developer secrets (~/.npmrc tokens, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/* keys, gh-cli token) that lived on the box. 3) Hunt: pivot on the package name across all `DeviceProcessEvents` org-wide for the last 30 days; pull `DeviceNetworkEvents` from affected hosts for outbound to GitHub/Bun/raw.githubusercontent.com/webhook.site; alert security team to remove the package version from internal mirrors.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npm-cli.js","npx.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bun.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","trufflehog.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\npx.exe","npm-cli.js")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\bun.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\trufflehog.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Suspicious child process spawned by npm or node during package install
id: 8b3e2a40-5c2d-4f8a-9a2c-1f7b4c5a6e9d
status: experimental
description: Detects npm/yarn/pnpm/node spawning a shell, downloader LOLBin, or known supply-chain tool (bun, trufflehog), indicating postinstall script abuse as seen in Nx s1ngularity, Shai-Hulud, and axios hijack campaigns.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-v12-block-postinstall

tags:

logsource:

detection:
  selection_parent:

      - '\npm.exe'

  selection_child:

  - electron-builder, husky, lerna spawning shells in build/git-hook flows
  - CI runners (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) where npm scripts shell out
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\YARN.EXE OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\PNPM.EXE OR *\\npx.exe OR *\\NPX.EXE) @Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\PWSH.EXE OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\bash.exe OR *\\BASH.EXE OR *\\sh.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE OR *\\wget.exe OR *\\WGET.EXE OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\BUN.EXE OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\BITSADMIN.EXE OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\CERTUTIL.EXE OR *\\trufflehog.exe OR *\\TRUFFLEHOG.EXE)

| ParentBaseFileName=/^(npm|node|yarn|pnpm|npx)(\.exe)?$/i

Bun runtime dropped or executed by node/npm child process (Shai-Hulud signature) AIInstallation High
Detects the Shai-Hulud and Mini Shai-Hulud signature: an npm install lifecycle script downloading and executing the Bun runtime to bootstrap a second-stage payload. Pre-Shai-Hulud, no benign npm package required pulling Bun mid-install. Rationale: Article explicitly states: 'Shai-Hulud ... installed the Bun runtime during setup' and Mini Shai-Hulud 'preinstall hook that pulled the Bun runtime'. The behaviour is article-specific: a benign npm package has no reason to drop bun.exe during install. Parent-restriction to node/npm/curl/wget eliminates the FP of a dev explicitly running `iwr bun.sh/install.ps1 | iex` from a shell of their own.
ATT&CKT1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing Bun globally via `npm install -g bun` (parent will be npm but child path likely `npm-global/bun.exe`)
  • Polyglot project that uses Bun as a declared dev-dependency and bootstraps it in postinstall
  • Container build steps in dev workstations using `bun` as the runtime
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in ("known-bun-developer1","known-bun-developer2") and FolderPath has_any ("npm-cache","\\AppData\\Roaming\\npm","\\.bun\\bin\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent npm install command — which package and version triggered the bun.exe write? Cross-reference against the host's package.json / package-lock.json — was bun a declared dependency? If yes and the user is a known Bun-using developer, downgrade. If no, treat as compromise. 2) Contain: isolate the host. Capture bun.exe, the parent package's tarball from node_modules cache, and any subsequently-spawned process. Rotate developer secrets (npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH). 3) Hunt: across the org, query `DeviceFileEvents` for any bun.exe write in the last 30 days with non-Bun-developer accounts; pivot the source npm package name and search for it in every package-lock.json / yarn.lock in source control.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog credential scanner executed from node/npm context AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Shai-Hulud secret-harvest signature: a node/npm/bun child process invoking trufflehog to scrape secrets. TruffleHog is a legitimate scanner, but executed by npm-install descent it indicates the Shai-Hulud (or copy-cat) credential-stealer phase. Rationale: Article explicitly: 'Shai-Hulud ... ran TruffleHog to scrape secrets, and dumped them into public GitHub repos.' TruffleHog under an npm parent is genuinely article-specific to that worm family — it's not in the generic supply-chain template. Parent restriction (node/npm/bun) eliminates the legit-security-tool FP path.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running TruffleHog as a pre-commit hook installed via husky (parent will be node.exe/git.exe)
  • GitGuardian or Trufflehog Enterprise agent on developer workstations
  • CI/CD pipeline running trufflehog as a scheduled SAST scan stage
  • Developer manually running `trufflehog filesystem .` from VS Code integrated terminal (parent powershell.exe / cmd.exe)
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in ("sec-eng-svc","trufflehog-runner") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("husky","lint-staged",".github/workflows","gitguardian"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user is NOT on the security team. Pull parent of parent — was this triggered by `npm install <package>`? Capture the package name and version. Pull trufflehog's command-line args to see what was scanned (`/`, `~`, `/etc`, GitHub orgs). 2) Contain: isolate host, kill any trufflehog process, force-rotate every credential type trufflehog defaults to scanning (GitHub PAT, npm tokens, AWS keys, SSH keys, GCP service account JSONs). Revoke npm publish tokens for any package the user maintains. 3) Hunt: check `DeviceNetworkEvents` and CloudTrail/GitHub audit logs for any new public-repo creates under the user's GitHub account in the last 7 days (Shai-Hulud's exfil pattern). Search the npm package on internal mirrors and remove.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("trufflehog.exe","trufflehog") or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","bun.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName has "trufflehog" or CommandLine has "trufflehog")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\npm.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\npx.exe","\\bun.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\bash.exe","\\sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network connection to npm supply-chain attack IOCs (sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73 / webhook.site) AICommand & Control Medium
Flags any host reaching the article's pre-extracted C2/exfil IOCs. webhook.site is a legitimate testing service frequently abused as an exfil sink by npm supply-chain worms; the IP and domain are tied to recent campaigns. Rationale: Pre-extracted IOC list for this article: 142.11.206.73, sfrclak.com, webhook.site. Webhook.site is named in the article context as a common exfil pivot for npm postinstall worms. Detection is the article's own infra, no template overlap. Confidence is Medium because the IOCs are from upstream pre-extraction rather than directly visible in the article body — recommend independent corroboration before tier-1 alerting.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backend engineer using webhook.site for legitimate webhook integration testing
  • QA testing third-party SaaS webhook integrations
  • Internal IT automation that uses webhook.site as a free debug endpoint
  • Stripe/Twilio/Slack integration testing where webhook.site is a common destination
  • Marketing teams using webhook.site for tracking-pixel debugging
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "webhook.site" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","postman.exe","insomnia.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (`InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine`). If node/npm/yarn — treat as confirmed compromise. If browser — likely benign QA. If powershell/curl — investigate the parent process chain. 2) Contain: if process is node/npm-related, isolate the host and revoke developer secrets (rotate npm tokens, GitHub PAT, AWS keys, SSH). Block 142.11.206.73 and *.sfrclak.com at the egress proxy. Add webhook.site to a 'business-justification-required' egress category rather than outright block. 3) Hunt: pivot on the package name (recovered from npm install command line) across all hosts for the last 30 days; search source control for any package.json referencing it; check GitHub audit logs for unusual public repo creates in the user's org (Shai-Hulud exfil pattern).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "142.11.206.73"
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("sfrclak.com","webhook.site")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP == "142.11.206.73" or DestinationHostName has_any ("sfrclak.com","webhook.site") or RequestURL has_any ("sfrclak.com","webhook.site")
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DeviceVendor),
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has_any ("sfrclak.com","webhook.site")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType),
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstIpAddr == "142.11.206.73" or DstHostname has_any ("sfrclak.com","webhook.site")
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm install with --ignore-scripts override bypassing v12 postinstall protection AIWeaponization Medium
After npm v12 lands (July 2026), the default is to block postinstall scripts unless allowlisted. Attackers and naive CI configs will attempt to re-enable scripts via `--ignore-scripts=false`, `npm_config_ignore_scripts=false`, or by gating on `--allow-git`/`--allow-remote` to revive remote/git execution paths. Flags use of these on hosts where the v12 default should hold. Rationale: Article calls out the new v12 controls explicitly: `--allow-git` (re-enables git deps) and `--allow-remote` (re-enables https-tarball deps) are the documented escape hatches; `--ignore-scripts=false` and the env-var equivalent are the obvious attacker pivots to re-enable postinstall on a v12 host. Each flag is verbatim from the article. Detection isn't a generic 'suspicious cmdline' — it's anchored to the exact defenses v12 introduces.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Monorepo builds with internal git-protocol dependencies (legitimately need --allow-git)
  • Air-gapped builds pulling from a self-hosted internal npm mirror over https (--allow-remote)
  • Developer rebuilding a native-module package locally where postinstall is required for compilation
  • CI jobs migrating from v11 → v12 that haven't yet committed an `allow-scripts.json` and are temporarily disabling the gate
  • Docker base-image builds that pre-warm node_modules
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("Agent.Worker.exe","actions-runner.exe","jenkins.exe","runner.exe","buildkite-agent.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--allow-git","--allow-remote"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host's npm version is v12+ (so the flag is actually a bypass and not pre-v12 noise). Identify the parent process — is it a CI runner, a user shell, or a script downloaded from the internet? Pull the install target package name from the same command line. 2) Contain: if parent is a downloaded script or non-IT-owned automation, isolate. If it's a known CI job, file a finding against the pipeline owner to migrate to `npm approve-scripts` rather than blanket-bypass. 3) Hunt: enumerate all hosts using these flags in the last 30 days and route to a remediation backlog; cross-reference with source control to find every CI yaml file embedding these flags; track adoption of the `allow-scripts` allowlist file across repos as the inverse signal.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","npm_config_ignore_scripts=false","npm_config_ignore_scripts=0","--allow-git","--allow-remote")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","npm_config_ignore_scripts=false","--allow-git","--allow-remote")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\npx.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\node.exe")
      or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\npx.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","npm_config_ignore_scripts=false","npm_config_ignore_scripts=0","--allow-git","--allow-remote")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known npm supply-chain malware hash observed on disk or in execution AIInstallation Medium
IOC sweep for the SHA1/SHA256 hashes pre-extracted from this article's IOC bundle - associated with the Nx s1ngularity, Shai-Hulud, axios hijack, and Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm campaigns. Hits indicate definitive presence of one of the named families. Rationale: Pre-extracted hashes from the article's IOC bundle - direct atomic indicators tied to the named campaigns. Hash matches are zero-FP. Unions process/file/image-load events so we catch the payload whether it executed, was dropped on disk, or was loaded as a side-load DLL. Confidence is High because hash-match is binary. Recommend cross-checking against threat intel before deploying as tier-1 alerts since the hashes come from upstream pre-extraction.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected for cryptographic hash matches against known-malicious samples
  • Possible: hash collisions are infeasible, but legitimate analyst submission of the sample to a sandbox running on a monitored host could fire
  • Possible: corporate threat-intel team detonating samples in an isolated VM where Defender ships hashes upstream
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox-","detonation-","ti-vm-") or AccountName in~ ("ti-analyst-svc","sandbox-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm this is not a security-team sandbox detonation (check `AccountName`, `DeviceName` against the IR/threat-intel VM allowlist). If not sandbox-attributed, treat as confirmed compromise. Pull the parent process chain and identify the source npm package + version that delivered this binary. 2) Contain: isolate host immediately. Block all the IOC IPs/domains from UC4 at the egress proxy. Force-rotate every credential the user could have touched: npm publish tokens, GitHub PAT, AWS keys, SSH keys, GCP service accounts, cloud provider session tokens. Pull the user's npm-published packages and audit recent releases for backdoor commits. 3) Hunt: org-wide hash sweep over 60 days; pull the source npm package name from the install command and grep every package.json/package-lock.json/yarn.lock in source control; alert security ops + remove the package from internal mirrors; report to npm security team.

union
  (DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (MaliciousSHA256) or SHA1 in (MaliciousSHA1) | project Timestamp, Source="Process", DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:

detection:

ENDPOINT

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated POST to Meta Ads MCP /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 AIDelivery High
Detects unauthenticated POST requests to the Meta Ads MCP /mcp endpoint on TCP 8080 that return HTTP 200, the exact exploitation primitive of CVE-2026-48039. Per the advisory, AuthInjectionMiddleware.dispatch() falls through to call_next() when no auth headers are present, so any 200 response to a POST /mcp without an Authorization or x-pipeboard-token header indicates exploitation. Rationale: Targets the exact exploitation signal called out in the advisory: POST /mcp on port 8080 returning 200 without an Authorization or x-pipeboard-token header. Cross-checked against the GHSA page and NVD entry for CVE-2026-48039. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48039

  • Load balancer pre-flight OPTIONS becoming POST via misconfigured probes
  • Internal observability tooling (Prometheus blackbox exporter) scraping /mcp
  • Developers smoke-testing the endpoint from corporate workstations
  • Penetration testers running authorized assessments

Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination host is running meta-ads-mcp <=1.0.108; pull the full POST body from proxy/WAF to identify which MCP tool was invoked (look for tools/call method names like get_ad_accounts). 2) Contain: block inbound TCP 8080 from untrusted sources at the perimeter, then rotate the META_ACCESS_TOKEN env var on the affected container and invalidate the leaked token in Meta Business Suite. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP for additional /mcp hits in the last 30d, search outbound traffic from the MCP host to graph.facebook.com for token-bearing URLs, and review Meta Graph API audit logs for any actions taken with the leaked token.

| order by Timestamp desc

MCP JSON-RPC tools/call payload posted to /mcp endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Detects POST requests to the Meta Ads MCP /mcp endpoint carrying a JSON-RPC tools/call payload — the request shape the advisory's PoC uses to invoke get_ad_accounts and trigger token leakage. Pairing the URL pattern with the JSON-RPC method=tools/call body signature distinguishes attacker tool invocation from idle TCP probes. Rationale: Targets the JSON-RPC tools/call payload shape directly shown in the article's PoC (method=tools/call, name=get_ad_accounts) — narrower than a flat URL-only match. Confirmed via GHSA advisory body PoC block. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate operator using the MCP client to query their own ad accounts
  • Authorized internal Postman/curl smoke tests against /mcp
  • Pipeboard SaaS health checks probing the JSON-RPC interface
  • CI pipeline integration tests posting tools/call payloads
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the JSON-RPC method and tool name from the body — get_ad_accounts, get_insights, create_campaign indicate ad-account enumeration or modification; check whether the source IP matches a known operator console. 2) Contain: if source is external/untrusted, block at WAF and rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN immediately. 3) Hunt: trace the response chain to graph.facebook.com over the next 60s; pull any error responses where request_url contains access_token=; confirm the leaked token was revoked in Meta Business Suite.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8080
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("meta_ads_mcp", "meta-ads-mcp")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "tools/call"
       or ProcessCommandLine has "get_ad_accounts"
       or ProcessCommandLine has "jsonrpc"
    | project DeviceId, ChildPid = ProcessId, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, ChildTime = Timestamp
) on DeviceId
| where ChildTime between (Timestamp .. Timestamp + 5s)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, LocalPort, ChildCmd,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Meta access_token query string leaked in HTTP response body from /mcp AIActions on Objectives High
Detects HTTP responses from the /mcp endpoint whose JSON body contains the literal access_token= URL fragment from a graph.facebook.com URL — the exact data leak path described in the advisory (api.py:263-269 serialising the raw httpx request_url into the JSON-RPC response). Requires proxy/WAF/NDR that captures response bodies. Rationale: Targets the precise leakage shape in the advisory PoC: the JSON-RPC response from /mcp embeds a request_url string that contains graph.facebook.com plus access_token=<value>. Three literal anchors keep FPs low. Defender / Falcon left blank because neither inspects HTTP response bodies natively. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory body. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/287.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Security researcher reproducing the PoC in a sandbox
  • Vulnerability scanner emitting matching strings as part of an active CVE-2026-48039 check
  • Internal incident-response replay of captured exploit traffic
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the leaked token from the captured response body and confirm it matches the value of META_ACCESS_TOKEN configured on the affected meta-ads-mcp instance; identify the unauthenticated client IP. 2) Contain: invalidate the leaked Meta access token in Meta Business Suite immediately, rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN in the container env, and block the client IP at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: pivot on the leaked token value across egress proxy logs for any subsequent direct calls to graph.facebook.com from external IPs, and audit Meta Graph API for ad-account changes within the token's validity window.

Meta Graph API call carrying access_token in URL query string from non-MCP host AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound HTTPS requests to graph.facebook.com that include access_token= in the URL but originate from a host or process that is NOT the meta-ads-mcp service. After exfiltrating the operator token via CVE-2026-48039, an attacker typically uses it directly against the Graph API from external infrastructure — this catches that follow-on usage. Rationale: Targets the article's described follow-on path — token leaked from /mcp gets used by the attacker directly against graph.facebook.com from infrastructure outside the operator's MCP deployment. Excludes the legitimate meta-ads-mcp process and standard browsers to surface CLI / scripted abuse. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory PoC URL pattern (https://graph.facebook.com/v24.0/me/adaccounts?...&access_token=...). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr

Meta Ads account admin or campaign modification via stolen access_token AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects high-impact Meta Graph API actions (add_admin, assign_role, create/modify campaign, update payment) initiated through API clients that don't match the operator's normal meta-ads-mcp identity — the lateral-movement step an attacker takes once they have exfiltrated the operator's META_ACCESS_TOKEN. Requires Meta Business Suite audit log forwarding into the SIEM (Cloud App Security / Defender for Cloud Apps connector). Rationale: Targets the lateral-movement step the advisory implies (impact follow-on to token leak): once the attacker holds META_ACCESS_TOKEN they pivot into account admin / campaign modification via Meta Graph API. UA exclusion of meta_ads_mcp / pipeboard surfaces the unexpected client. Cross-checked against MITRE ATT&CK T1098.001 (Additional Cloud Credentials) and T1550.001 (Application Access Token). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9gw6-46qc-99vr • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/001/
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication Change
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing manager performing legitimate role changes via Meta Business Suite web UI
  • Authorized agency partner being granted account access on a planned campaign launch
  • Internal automation script that uses the Graph API directly (bypassing MCP) and has its own approved user agent
  • Meta Business Suite mobile app calls that don't carry the MCP UA
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the calling identity matches an expected business user; review the IP geolocation and ISP for the action, and compare against the operator's known IP ranges. 2) Contain: revoke the access token used for the action in Meta Business Suite, remove any newly-added admins or roles, and rotate META_ACCESS_TOKEN on every meta-ads-mcp instance. 3) Hunt: pull 30 days of Meta Graph API audit for the affected ad accounts, look for campaign / payment-method changes and budget movements, and correlate with prior alerts on unauthenticated POST /mcp activity to confirm root cause.

Miasma worm GitHub commit-search C2 magic strings on command line or script AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the three hard-coded GitHub commit-search query strings the Miasma supply-chain worm uses as its three independent C2 channels (PAT discovery, JavaScript payload delivery, Python payload delivery). These strings have zero legitimate business presence and are the highest-fidelity Miasma indicator available. Rationale: The three strings 'DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom', 'TheBeautifulSandsOfTime' and 'firedalazer' are the hard-coded GitHub commit-search queries each Miasma C2 channel uses (PAT discovery, JS payload, Python payload). They are confirmed by SafeDep's analysis, BleepingComputer's report, and a parallel TheHackerNews write-up. Zero legitimate business processes contain these tokens. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-supply-chain-attack-compromises.html • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002 T1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst running these strings through their own grep/search tooling for hunting
  • SOC engineer pasting the IOCs into a script or note file
  • Security researcher cloning or reading SafeDep / Cloudsmith write-ups in a developer IDE that logs URL paths
  • Sandbox / detonation environment intentionally executing a Miasma sample for analysis
  • Automation that ingests OSS-supply-chain advisories and writes IOCs to a database column
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("misp.exe","opencti.exe") and not (FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\","\\detonation\\","\\analyst-tools\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process that emitted the string is not an analyst hunting tool, a CTI ingestion script, or a known sandbox. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain; if the string was in a network URL, identify what process issued the GET against api.github.com/search/commits. 2) Contain: if the originating process is a node/python/git/curl invocation on a developer machine or CI runner, isolate the host from network, revoke any GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems publish tokens and JFrog Artifactory credentials owned by that user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the same three strings org-wide; pivot on the parent process and SHA256 to find sibling executions; review the developer's git push history for npm/PyPI/RubyGems package versions published in the last 7d for unexpected new releases or postinstall scripts.
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256 = InitiatingProcessSHA256, Source = strcat("Net:", RemoteUrl);
union ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaC2 = dynamic(["DontRevokeOrItGoesBoom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (MiasmaC2)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
union From4688, FromAsim
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma supply-chain worm leaked repo clone, install or fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts for git clone / npm install / pip install / curl / wget operations that reference the briefly-public 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' GitHub repositories which leaked the worm's source on 2026-06-08. A match means the host has either ingested the leaked toolkit or is being staged with it. Rationale: 'Miasma-Open-Source-Release' is the exact repository slug SafeDep and BleepingComputer report appeared on GitHub from 2026-06-08 hosting the leaked toolkit. The string is uniquely tied to Miasma and would only surface in dev-tool command lines or proxy URLs when a host is cloning, installing or downloading the leaked source. Cross-checked via SafeDep, BleepingComputer and TheRegister. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/the-miasma-worm-source-code-briefly-leaked-on-github/ • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://cloudsmith.com/blog/miasma-worms-path-of-destruction
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1105 T1588.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel team intentionally cloning the leaked repo into a sandbox for analysis
  • Security researcher fetching the source on a developer workstation for write-up
  • SOAR / TIP ingesting OSS advisory feeds and storing the repo URL as an IOC string
  • Vulnerability scanner or SCA tool fingerprinting against known-malicious repo names
  • Blue-team CTF or training environment seeding the toolkit deliberately
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\") and FolderPath !has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\detonation\\", "\\malware-analysis\\", "\\threat-intel\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and parent process that issued the clone/install/fetch — confirm it is not a sanctioned analyst sandbox or CTI ingestion job. Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and any subsequent npm/pip postinstall script execution from the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node/python child processes spawned within 1 hour of the clone, revoke GitHub PATs and SSH keys cached on it, and rotate npm/PyPI/RubyGems/Artifactory publish tokens belonging to the user. 3) Hunt: search 30d for the three Miasma C2 commit-search strings (see related UC) on the same host and across the org; review the user's recent package publishes for unexpected versions; check GitHub Actions workflows in any repo they touched for newly-added steps referencing untrusted secrets or external scripts.
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let DevTools = dynamic(["git.exe","npm.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","git","npm","node","pip","python","python3","curl","wget"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ (DevTools) or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (DevTools)
    | where ProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, Source = "Process";
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl contains MiasmaRepo
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "Network";
union isfuzzy=true ProcHits, NetHits
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| order by Timestamp desc
let MiasmaRepo = "Miasma-Open-Source-Release";
let From4688 = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source = "4688";
let FromAsim = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo or TargetProcessCommandLine contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, Account = ActorUsername, NewProcessName = TargetProcessName, CommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName, Source = "ASIM";
let FromProxy = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL contains MiasmaRepo or DestinationHostName contains MiasmaRepo
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, Account = SourceUserName, NewProcessName = "", CommandLine = RequestURL, ParentProcessName = "", Source = "Proxy";
union From4688, FromAsim, FromProxy
| where Account !endswith "$"
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("kernel32.dll", "charmap.exe", "router.elf", "version.dll", "inspect.sys"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FileName in~ ("kernel32.dll", "charmap.exe", "router.elf", "version.dll", "inspect.sys"))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] FireAnt Metakit supply-chain: update binary spawning unusual child
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OceanLotus: From external espionage to domestic targeting
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SPECTRALVIPER known-sample SHA1 execution or filesystem write · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 connection to ESET-disclosed IPs/domains · [LLM] First-seen connection to recently-registered SPECTRALVIPER-shape C2 domain · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
OceanLotus SPECTRALVIPER C2 connection to ESET-disclosed IPs/domains AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound network connection to the eight SPECTRALVIPER C2 IPs and six C&C domains ESET published for OceanLotus's 2024-2026 FireAnt Metakit supply-chain and Vietnamese construction-corp campaigns. High-fidelity because every IOC is a known-bad C2 endpoint with no documented benign use. Rationale: Every IP and domain in this query is a SPECTRALVIPER C&C endpoint published in ESET's Table 2 and IOC bundle for the 2024-2026 OceanLotus campaigns; financemachinelearning.com is explicitly named as the C&C domain for the stable SPECTRALVIPER variant. Match by IP catches direct fallback; match by URL catches HTTPS proxied through hostname.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox / malware-analysis VM intentionally detonating SPECTRALVIPER samples
  • Threat-intel scrapers / Shodan-style researchers actively probing the IOC set
  • Security-tool URL-categorization scans of the malicious domains (e.g. Zscaler, Netskope)
  • Legitimate hosts that happen to be on a shared-IP CDN that now resolves to one of these IPs (rare — most IOCs are bare hosting)
  • DNS sinkhole responses if these domains have been sinkholed by a TI provider
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","iexplore.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full process tree from DeviceProcessEvents for InitiatingProcessFileName at the time of the connection — confirm whether the originator is a known good binary (security tooling, sandbox) or an unsigned binary in a temp/AppData path matching SPECTRALVIPER drop patterns. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the device via Defender Live Response or EDR network-isolation, block the matched IP/domain at firewall and EDR network indicator policy, force credential reset for the InitiatingProcessAccountName. 3) HUNT: pivot on DeviceFileEvents for SHA1 against the 20-hash IOC set; query DnsEvents for the other five C&C domains across all hosts in the last 90 days; search for any FireAnt Metakit installs (file path or process name) on neighboring hosts and check their update history for a malicious payload window of Oct-2025 to Mar-2026.

let ioc_domains = dynamic(["financemachinelearning.com","gatewayrvcenter.com","coachcybersecurity.com","mxprodesign.com","power-sync-services.com","leadingfilipinoteams.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (ioc_ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (ioc_domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

(ImNetworkSession

  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url, EventProduct),
(CommonSecurityLog
