Burst of JWT validation failures (401/403) on go-base /api/v1/* endpoints from single source AIExploitation Medium
Detects token-forgery probing against a go-base-style API: an attacker with the leaked 'random' secret will iterate JWT claims (sub, roles, exp) until validation passes. Each iteration that misses produces a 401 or 403 from the jwtauth middleware. A sustained burst from one source IP — especially against the article-named paths — is the failed-forgery footprint. Rationale: Anchored on the exact endpoint prefix /api/v1/ used in the article PoC. The 401/403 pair is what go-chi/jwtauth/v5 returns when signature verification fails or when the resolved roles don't satisfy the route's RequireRole — the two failure modes a forgery attacker iterates through. Threshold of 20 in 5m is empirical for noisy probing while staying above legitimate expired-token churn. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
ATT&CKT1606 T1110.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile or SPA client with an expired refresh-token loop hammering /api/v1/me
  • Synthetic monitoring (Pingdom, Datadog Synthetics) probing the API without valid auth
  • Pen-test or DAST scanner (Burp, ZAP) run against the staging API
  • Misconfigured CI job using a stale JWT in its smoke test
  • Authenticated user crossing token-rotation window during a deploy
Suppression filter
| where UA !has "Pingdom" and UA !has "Datadog Synthetics" and UA !has "StatusCake" and UA !has "UptimeRobot"
| where not (UA has "python-requests" and Host has "-dev")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the burst's full request set — are the 401/403s clustered on /api/v1/admin/* and /api/v1/token/refresh (PoC pattern) or scattered? Look at the User-Agent: legitimate clients are consistent; forgery probes often rotate or use `python-requests/*` matching the article PoC. 2) CONTAIN: WAF-block the source IP at the edge if non-corporate; if the host serves go-base, rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET immediately and invalidate sessions. Run UC1 against the backing host to confirm whether it shipped with the hardcoded default. 3) HUNT: pivot to UC3 with the same source IP — if a 200 follows the burst on /api/v1/admin/*, treat as confirmed exploitation. Pull DB audit logs for any data accessed by the forged session.
let WindowMinutes = 5m;
let FailureThreshold = 20;
union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
   | where csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/"
   | where scStatus in (401, 403)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIp = cIP, Host = sSiteName, Uri = csUriStem,
             Status = scStatus, UA = csUserAgent, Method = csMethod),
  (AppServiceHTTPLogs
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
   | where CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/"
   | where ScStatus in (401, 403)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIp = CIp, Host = CsHost, Uri = CsUriStem,
             Status = ScStatus, UA = UserAgent, Method = CsMethod),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
   | where RequestURL has "/api/v1/"
   | where EventOutcome in ("401", "403")
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIp = SourceIP, Host = DestinationHostName,
             Uri = RequestURL, Status = toint(EventOutcome),
             UA = RequestClientApplication, Method = RequestMethod)
| summarize FailedAttempts = count(),
            UniquePaths = dcount(Uri),
            SamplePaths = make_set(Uri, 8),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIp, Host, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where FailedAttempts >= FailureThreshold
| order by LastSeen desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.status=401 OR Web.status=403) AND (Web.url="*/api/v1/*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats sum(count) as Failures dc(url) as UniquePaths values(url) as Paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest
| where Failures >= 20
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - Failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.status=401 OR Web.status=403) AND (Web.url="*/api/v1/*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats sum(count) as Failures dc(url) as UniquePaths values(url) as Paths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest
| where Failures >= 20
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - Failures
go-base admin/refresh endpoint hit without preceding successful login from same source AIActions on Objectives Medium
After an attacker forges a JWT with AUTH_JWT_SECRET='random', they skip the login flow entirely and hit /api/v1/admin/users or /api/v1/token/refresh directly. Legitimate users always traverse the login endpoint first. Surfaces successful forged-token use by anti-joining admin/refresh hits against recent successful logins from the same source IP. Rationale: The article PoC explicitly shows the attacker skipping the login step — `requests.get('/api/v1/admin/users')` and `requests.post('/api/v1/token/refresh')` with only a forged Authorization header. Anti-joining admin hits against logins on the same source IP catches exactly that footprint. Endpoints are the literal paths named in the PoC code block. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mqq6-462x-jxmm
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Service-to-service API client using a long-lived bearer token (no human login flow)
  • Mobile app resuming a stored refresh token after >30 minutes of inactivity
  • NAT egress IP where one user logged in and another reaches admin paths
  • API key / PAT auth that bypasses /login by design
  • SSO callback flow where the login endpoint sits on a different host than the API
Suppression filter
| where UA !has "okhttp" and UA !has "Darwin/" and UA !has "Android"
| where UA !has "GoogleHC" and UA !has "kube-probe"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the full request set for the source IP — does the UA / TLS fingerprint match a known mobile or service client? Check whether the AdminUri is /api/v1/admin/users specifically (the PoC path) versus a benign admin route. Validate against UC1 — was the backing host running with AUTH_JWT_SECRET=random? 2) CONTAIN: revoke the offending session/token at the API; if confirmed forged, rotate AUTH_JWT_SECRET to a 32-byte random value (`openssl rand -base64 32`) and force re-auth for all users. Block source IP at the WAF. 3) HUNT: search the DB / app audit logs for actions taken under the forged identity (the PoC creates an admin@example.com sub claim — look for any sub value not present in the user table). Pivot on UA across the org to find other IPs using the same forgery toolkit.
let LookbackHours = 2h;
let LoginWindowSec = 1800;
let AdminHits =
  union isfuzzy=true
    (W3CIISLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
     | where csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/admin/" or csUriStem matches regex @"^/api/v1/token/refresh"
     | where scStatus == 200
     | project AdminTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp = cIP, AdminUri = csUriStem,
               UA = csUserAgent, Host = sSiteName),
    (AppServiceHTTPLogs
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
     | where CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/admin/" or CsUriStem matches regex @"^/api/v1/token/refresh"
     | where ScStatus == 200
     | project AdminTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp = CIp, AdminUri = CsUriStem,
               UA = UserAgent, Host = CsHost);
let LoginEvents =
  union isfuzzy=true
    (W3CIISLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours + 1h)
     | where csUriStem in ("/api/v1/login", "/api/v1/auth/login", "/login", "/oauth/token")
     | where scStatus == 200
     | project LoginTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp = cIP),
    (AppServiceHTTPLogs
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours + 1h)
     | where CsUriStem in ("/api/v1/login", "/api/v1/auth/login", "/login", "/oauth/token")
     | where ScStatus == 200
     | project LoginTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIp = CIp);
AdminHits
| join kind=leftouter LoginEvents on SrcIp
| extend HasRecentLogin = isnotempty(LoginTime)
         and datetime_diff('second', AdminTime, LoginTime) between (0 .. LoginWindowSec)
| summarize HasRecentLogin = max(HasRecentLogin),
            AdminHits = dcount(AdminTime),
            Endpoints = make_set(AdminUri, 10),
            UAs = make_set(UA, 5),
            FirstHit = min(AdminTime),
            LastHit = max(AdminTime)
          by SrcIp, Host
| where HasRecentLogin == false
| order by LastHit desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.status=200 AND (Web.url="*/api/v1/admin/*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/token/refresh*") by Web.src Web.url _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename _time as admin_time
| join type=left src [
    | tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.status=200 AND (Web.url="*/api/v1/login*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/auth/login*" OR Web.url="*/login*" OR Web.url="*/oauth/token*") by Web.src _time
    | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
    | stats max(_time) as last_login by src ]
| where isnull(last_login) OR (admin_time - last_login) > 1800
| eval login_gap_min = round((admin_time - coalesce(last_login,0))/60, 1)
| table admin_time src url login_gap_min last_login
| sort - admin_time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.status=200 AND (Web.url="*/api/v1/admin/*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/token/refresh*") by Web.src Web.url _time
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename _time as admin_time
| join type=left src [
    | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.status=200 AND (Web.url="*/api/v1/login*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/auth/login*" OR Web.url="*/login*" OR Web.url="*/oauth/token*") by Web.src _time
    | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
    | stats max(_time) as last_login by src ]
| where isnull(last_login) OR (admin_time - last_login) > 1800
| eval login_gap_min = round((admin_time - coalesce(last_login,0))/60, 1)
| table admin_time src url login_gap_min last_login
| sort - admin_time
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48031")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48031")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Compromised Rust crate onering performs code exfiltration

Aikido
2026-06-10 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The compromised onering Rust crate v1.4.1 on crates.io shipped a malicious build.rs that exfiltrates the diff of your latest commit to a hosted Sentry endpoint every time you build. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] onering 1.4.1 crate landing in cargo registry cache (compromised-version install)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound POST to onering crate C2 Sentry ingest endpoint (o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io) · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Outbound POST to onering crate C2 Sentry ingest endpoint (o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io) AICommand & Control High
Detects network connections from any process to the specific Sentry ingest endpoint used by the malicious onering 1.4.1 crate to exfiltrate git diffs. The domain/org/project ID combination is unique to this campaign and any contact from a development machine indicates compromised build pipeline. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact IOCs: the full Sentry ingest hostname o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io, the project path /4511539669368912/envelope/, and the DSN public key 8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821. All three are unique to this attacker's tenant so contact = compromise — no need to baseline.
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security researcher reproducing the malicious build.rs in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel platform actively fetching the URL for IOC enrichment
  • Aikido's own scanner crawling the endpoint during a customer demo
  • DFIR analyst manually testing the indicator from their workstation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")  // exclude browser-based research lookups
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "aikido" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ioc-research"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the source host and the initiating process — confirm it's a developer workstation/CI runner and look for nearby cargo/rustc/build-script-build activity in DeviceProcessEvents within ±10 minutes of the network event. Pull the dev's Cargo.lock and grep for `onering = "1.4.1"`. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill cargo/build processes, rotate any git credentials and SSH/PAT tokens stored on the box, force a fresh clone of every active repo. Treat the contents of the most recent commit diff on each affected repo as leaked. 3) HUNT: Across all dev/CI estate, run `Get-Content **/Cargo.lock | Select-String 'onering'`. Pivot on Sentry org id `o4511539639222272` for any related campaign infrastructure and check git log for any onering references in branch dependencies pulled from the GitHub mirror.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
   or RemoteUrl has "4511539669368912/envelope"
   or RemoteUrl has "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io", "4511539669368912/envelope", "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpUserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname
| union (
    ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstHostname has "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io"
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

curl POSTing Sentry envelope payload from cargo/build-script-build context AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the article's specific exfiltration shape: curl invoked with the malicious Sentry envelope URL and/or DSN, where the parent is a Rust build artifact (cargo, rustc, build-script-build). Catches the same exfil even if RemoteUrl is blocked at the proxy. Rationale: Pivots on three article-extracted strings that, together, can't be a coincidence: the exact ingest URL path 4511539669368912/envelope/, the DSN public key 8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821, and the unusual Content-Type application/x-sentry-envelope literally shown in the request() call. Catches the exfil even when DNS is sinkholed.
ATT&CKT1059 T1105 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security testing reproducing the payload
  • Threat-intel automation probing the URL for liveness
  • DFIR analyst manually replaying the IOC
  • Aikido employee/customer testing the disclosed sample in a lab
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the parent chain — look for cargo / rustc / build-script-build / cargo build / cargo check several hops up. If the grandparent is a build script, treat as confirmed onering. 2) CONTAIN: Kill cargo and any background rust-analyzer/cargo-watch processes, isolate host, revoke all git PATs and SSH keys present on the box. The diff of the last commit on every active repo on that host should be considered exfiltrated. 3) HUNT: Search `DeviceProcessEvents | where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "build-script-build"` across the org for the last 30 days. Inventory Cargo.lock files for `onering` at any version and Cargo.toml files declaring it as a direct or transitive dependency.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","curl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io",
    "4511539669368912/envelope",
    "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821",
    "application/x-sentry-envelope"
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentName=InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandparentName=InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl.exe","/curl") or TargetProcessName has_any ("curl.exe","/curl")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (
    "o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io",
    "4511539669368912/envelope",
    "8197ee42c4f59c83f4cc6d48f5bae821",
    "application/x-sentry-envelope"
  )
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

Rust build script (build-script-build) executing 'git diff HEAD^ HEAD' for source-code harvesting AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the article's specific collection step: a Cargo-compiled build script binary spawning git to dump the latest commit diff. Legitimate build scripts rarely shell out to git, and `diff HEAD^ HEAD` is a code-stealing pattern, not a versioning pattern. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim git commands from the article (`git diff HEAD^ HEAD`) and the Cargo build-output path convention `target/{debug,release}/build/<pkg-hash>/build-script-build` — that parent identity is what makes this anomalous (build scripts almost never call git, and `HEAD^ HEAD` is specifically a one-commit-diff dump, not a versioning lookup). Works even if the attacker rotates the Sentry endpoint.
ATT&CKT1005 T1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate build scripts using vergen/git2 crates for version-stamping (usually call `git rev-parse` / `git log -1`, rarely `diff HEAD^ HEAD`)
  • Crates that legitimately embed changelog diffs as compile-time strings (rare)
  • Internal vendored crate that snapshots last commit into a binary for diagnostics
  • A custom crates.io mirror's verification tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("vergen", "git2-rs") and ProcessCommandLine has "rev-parse")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Get the full parent chain (cargo -> build-script-build -> git). Identify the source crate by inspecting the path segment after `target/debug/build/<crate-name>-<hash>/`. Match the crate name against the known compromise list (onering, plus anything sharing a maintainer). 2) CONTAIN: Kill cargo, isolate host, treat the diff of HEAD as exfiltrated for every git repo on the machine. Force credential rotation for any token/secret committed within the last commit window. 3) HUNT: Across the dev/CI fleet, run the same query without the 30d bound. Pull `Cargo.lock` from CI artifact storage and grep for `onering`. Block `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` at the egress proxy. Audit `~/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-*/onering-*/build.rs` on every host for the malicious payload.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe","git")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "diff"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "HEAD^" or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"HEAD\^?\s+HEAD"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "build-script-"
     or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "build_script_"
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\target\debug\build\"
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/target/debug/build/"
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\target\release\build\"
     or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "/target/release/build/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandparentName=InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("git.exe","/git") or ActingProcessName has_any ("git.exe","/git")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "diff" and TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"HEAD\^?\s+HEAD"
| where ActingProcessName startswith "build-script-"
     or ActingProcessName startswith "build_script_"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has @"\target\debug\build\"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has "/target/debug/build/"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has @"\target\release\build\"
     or ActingProcessCommandLine has "/target/release/build/"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Rust build.rs Artifact Spawning git diff HEAD^ HEAD
id: 6b1a4d3c-8e9f-4a2b-9c3d-5e7f8a1b2c3d
description: Cargo-compiled build script binary (under target/{debug,release}/build/) executing 'git diff HEAD^ HEAD' to harvest the most recent commit — the onering 1.4.1 supply-chain attack pattern.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-rust-crate-onering-performs-code-exfiltration
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1005
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_git:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\git.exe'
      - '/git'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'diff'
      - 'HEAD^'
      - 'HEAD'
  selection_parent_build_script:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - '\target\debug\build\'
      - '/target/debug/build/'
      - '\target\release\build\'
      - '/target/release/build/'
  selection_parent_name:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - 'build-script-build'
      - 'build_script_build'
      - 'build-script-main'
  condition: selection_git and (selection_parent_build_script or selection_parent_name)
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 AND @Image:(*\git.exe OR *\GIT.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*diff*HEAD^*HEAD* OR *"diff HEAD^ HEAD"*) AND @ParentImage:(*\target\debug\build\* OR *\target\release\build\* OR *build-script-build* OR *build_script_build*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.executable.path:*/git @process.command_line:*diff*HEAD^*HEAD* AND @process.parent.executable.path:(*/target/debug/build/* OR */target/release/build/*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/[\\\/]git(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("diff\\s+HEAD\\^?\\s+HEAD", field=CommandLine)
| (regex("[\\\\/]target[\\\\/](debug|release)[\\\\/]build[\\\\/]", field=ParentImageFileName) OR ParentBaseFileName=/^build[-_]script[-_](build|main)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentImageFileName, CommandLine], function=[count(), min(@timestamp)])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="git.exe" OR Processes.process_name="git") AND Processes.process="*diff*" AND Processes.process="*HEAD^*" AND Processes.process="*HEAD*" AND (Processes.parent_process_name="build-script-build*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="build_script_build*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="build-script-main*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\target\\debug\\build\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*/target/debug/build/*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\target\\release\\build\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*/target/release/build/*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="git.exe" OR Processes.process_name="git") AND Processes.process="*diff*" AND Processes.process="*HEAD^*" AND Processes.process="*HEAD*" AND (Processes.parent_process_name="build-script-build*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="build_script_build*" OR Processes.parent_process_name="build-script-main*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\target\\debug\\build\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*/target/debug/build/*" OR Processes.parent_process="*\\target\\release\\build\\*" OR Processes.parent_process="*/target/release/build/*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
onering 1.4.1 crate landing in cargo registry cache (compromised-version install) AIDelivery High
Detects the install footprint of the malicious crate: cargo writing onering-1.4.1 into ~/.cargo/registry/{cache,src}/. This is the earliest possible signal — before build.rs ever runs — and catches both fresh `cargo install` and `cargo build` against a Cargo.toml that pulled the bad version. Rationale: Anchored on the exact compromised version string `onering-1.4.1` from the article's IOC block and Cargo's well-documented registry layout (`~/.cargo/registry/{cache,src}/<index>/onering-<version>/`). Fires once per host on first install — before build.rs ever executes — giving the SOC the earliest possible kill point.
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher pulling the crate for analysis in an isolated VM
  • CI matrix specifically pinned to onering 1.4.1 for regression validation against the known-bad build
  • Mirror/proxy operator (e.g. Artifactory) syncing the bad version before it's been quarantined
  • Pre-blocklist replication: nightly cargo cache warmer that pulled 1.4.1 before disclosure
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("defender.exe","mssense.exe","avscan")  // exclude AV unpacking during scan
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the file landed (`~/.cargo/registry/cache/index.crates.io-*/onering-1.4.1.crate` or extracted source under `registry/src/.../onering-1.4.1/`). Check git history of any project that imports it. Pivot to DeviceProcessEvents to see whether `cargo build` / `cargo check` has executed yet — that's the trigger for build.rs. 2) CONTAIN: Block `o4511539639222272.ingest.de.sentry.io` at egress, delete the `onering-1.4.1` cache + src directories, pin `onering = "1.4.0"` (or pre-compromise version) in Cargo.toml and regenerate Cargo.lock. If `cargo build` already ran, treat HEAD diff of every repo on the host as leaked. 3) HUNT: Across the org, query DeviceFileEvents for `onering-1.4.1` over the last 90d; inventory all Cargo.lock files committed to source control for `name = "onering"` and `version = "1.4.1"`. Check the cenotelie/onering GitHub repo activity — pulling from git rather than crates.io does NOT mitigate per the article.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has @"\.cargo\registry\" or FolderPath has "/.cargo/registry/")
| where (FileName == "onering-1.4.1.crate")
     or (FolderPath has "onering-1.4.1" and FileName in~ ("build.rs","Cargo.toml","lib.rs"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (TargetFilePath has @"\.cargo\registry\" or TargetFilePath has "/.cargo/registry/")
| where (TargetFileName == "onering-1.4.1.crate")
     or (TargetFilePath has "onering-1.4.1" and TargetFileName in~ ("build.rs","Cargo.toml","lib.rs"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

10 year old critical vulnerability in phpBB affecting tens of millions of users across thousands of forums

Aikido
2026-06-10 3 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Aikido Security discovered a critical unauthenticated authentication bypass in phpBB affecting tens of millions of users. A single HTTP request is all it takes to take over any account — a vulnerability that's been sitting in the codebase since 2014. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

CVEsCVE-2026-29199
ATT&CKT1190 T1528

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable phpBB instances exposed to CVE-2026-29199 auth bypass / RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Vulnerable phpBB instances exposed to CVE-2026-29199 auth bypass / RCE AIExploitation High
Identifies devices hosting phpBB at or below the versions Aikido named as vulnerable (3.3.16 on the 3.x line, 4.0.0-a2 on the 4.x line). A single unauthenticated HTTP request yields a valid session as any user including admins, which on the latest 4.x line opens full RCE. Patch posture is the only article-grounded lever until technical detail is published. Rationale: Detection is bound to the exact strings the article names: CVE-2026-29199, the 3.3.16 / 4.0.0-a2 cap on vulnerable versions, and the 3.3.17 patched build. Aikido explicitly stated technical detail is withheld until administrators upgrade, so a behavioural HTTP / process / file-drop detection would be a fabricated generic template — skipped by design per the hard rules. No external sources cross-checked; the disclosure post-dates this writing and abuse.ch / NVD entries are not expected to carry payloads until Aikido's follow-up.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Test/staging phpBB instances intentionally pinned to a pre-3.3.17 version for migration testing
  • Vendor-supported phpBB derivative shipping its own version string (e.g. forked appliance build) that hasn't merged the upstream patch yet but is internally hardened
  • Defender TVM scan lag — host was upgraded to 3.3.17 in the last 24h but inventory hasn't refreshed
  • phpBB CLI install under a developer's home directory not exposed to the internet (low impact, still surfaces as vulnerable)
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion != "3.3.17"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the SoftwareVersion on the device matches what's actually deployed (ssh / config /includes/constants.php / phpBB ACP). Cross-check DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing or the external attack-surface inventory to score exposure. Step 2 — Contain: for any internet-exposed instance, push a WAF / reverse-proxy rule blocking unauthenticated requests to /ucp.php and /user/* until upgrade lands, and force-rotate admin session cookies (phpBB ACP > Security > clear all sessions); for internal instances, schedule upgrade in the next maintenance window. Step 3 — Hunt: pull 30 days of web-access logs for the affected vhost and bookmark them — when Aikido publishes the promised technical write-up, replay logs against the new IOC set to determine pre-disclosure exploitation.
let VulnerableInventory =
    DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
    | where SoftwareName has "phpbb"
    | extend Branch = case(SoftwareVersion startswith "3.", "3.x", SoftwareVersion startswith "4.", "4.x", "other")
    | where (Branch == "3.x" and SoftwareVersion != "3.3.17") or (Branch == "4.x" and SoftwareVersion in ("4.0.0-a1", "4.0.0-a2"));
let TaggedByMS =
    DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where CveId == "CVE-2026-29199";
VulnerableInventory
| join kind=fullouter TaggedByMS on DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, Branch, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 7d;
let ByCve =
    DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where CveId == "CVE-2026-29199";
let ByVersion =
    DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where SoftwareName has "phpbb"
    | where (SoftwareVersion startswith "3." and SoftwareVersion != "3.3.17") or SoftwareVersion in ("4.0.0-a1", "4.0.0-a2");
union ByCve, ByVersion
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pheditor CVE-2026-48030: shell metacharacters in 'dir' POST parameter to action=terminal AIExploitation High
Hunts the wire signature of the Pheditor terminal-handler command injection: a POST to pheditor.php with action=terminal where the dir parameter carries shell metacharacters (semicolon, pipe, backtick, $(, &&, or trailing #). The whitelist on `command` is bypassed via `dir`, so this is the cleanest pre-RCE indicator. Rationale: Article states the exact vulnerable wire shape: `action=terminal`, `dir=/tmp; curl ... #` — the semicolon and trailing comment are both literal PoC strings. We match raw and URL-encoded versions because the PoC uses --data-urlencode. HTTP 200 confirms the injection succeeded (the article shows `{"error":false,"message":"OK"}` returns 200).
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit pheditor admin pasting a path with spaces or special chars from a backup script
  • Security scanners (Nuclei, Burp scanner, Nessus) probing the CVE with the same payload — investigate but classify as testing
  • Internal pentest / red-team exercise against the pheditor instance
  • DevOps automation posting to action=terminal with directory paths that legitimately contain a hash character (uncommon but possible in misc dev environments)
Suppression filter
and not (cIP in ('<scanner-cidr>','<internal-pentest-host>') and csUserName in ('redteam','secscan'))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the full request body for the alerting requests (most WAF/proxy logs capture POST body). Confirm `action=terminal` AND `dir=` containing a shell metacharacter. Identify the authenticated user from the session/Authorization header and the source IP. Step 2 — Contain: Disable terminal permission for the suspected account in Pheditor settings, rotate that user's credentials, and block the source IP at the perimeter. If pheditor 2.0.1–2.0.3 is confirmed, take the app offline and upgrade — there is no in-app config that mitigates the bug without a patch. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the web server host for DeviceProcessEvents where php-fpm/apache spawned sh/bash/curl/wget in the last 7 days (UC2), .php files written under /var/www by the php-fpm UID (UC3), and HTTP GETs to any new .php in the webroot (UC4).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem endswith "/pheditor.php"
| where csMethod =~ "POST"
| where csUriQuery has "action=terminal" or csUriQuery has "dir="
| where csUriQuery matches regex @"dir=[^&]*(%3B|;|%7C|\||%26%26|&&|`|%60|\$\(|%24%28|%23|#)"
| where scStatus in ("200", "302")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUserName, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 Terminal Handler dir Parameter Command Injection
id: 9b3a8c1e-44e7-4f51-a2cb-7e1f4a02f9d0
description: Detects exploitation of CVE-2026-48030 against pheditor.php where shell metacharacters are passed in the 'dir' POST parameter to the terminal action handler, bypassing the TERMINAL_COMMANDS whitelist.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.004
  - cve.2026.48030
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_url:
    cs-method: POST
    cs-uri-stem|endswith: '/pheditor.php'
  selection_payload:
    cs-uri-query|contains:
      - 'action=terminal'
      - 'dir='
  selection_meta:
    cs-uri-query|re: 'dir=[^&]*(%3B|;|%7C|\||%26%26|&&|`|%60|\$\(|%24%28|%23|#)'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
(source:nginx.access OR source:apache.access) @http.method:POST @http.url:*pheditor.php* @http.status_code:(200 OR 302) (@http.url_details.queryString:*action=terminal* OR @http.useragent:*) (@http.url:*dir=*%3B* OR @http.url:*dir=*%7C* OR @http.url:*dir=*%26%26* OR @http.url:*dir=*%60* OR @http.url:*dir=*%24%28* OR @http.url:*dir=*%23*)
WEB

PHP/web-server parent spawning shell utilities (Pheditor RCE post-exploitation) AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation shell chain produced by CVE-2026-48030: php-fpm / httpd / nginx / apache2 parent process spawning sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, or python. The TERMINAL_COMMANDS whitelist is bypassed via the `dir` injection, so any utility outside the whitelist showing up as a child of the web-server account on a pheditor host is high-signal. Rationale: Article's PoC walks www-data shell-spawning twice: `curl -s https://ifconfig.me` via `dir=/tmp; curl ... #`, then `echo '<?php ...' > shell.php`. The bypass article literally names www-data (`uid=33(www-data)`) as the post-exploit identity. Filtering on web-user account + shell child + web-server parent is article-grounded, not generic.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1548
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PHP applications using shell_exec() for image conversion (ImageMagick wrappers calling sh)
  • Composer post-install scripts running curl during deploy (parent is usually cli php, not php-fpm — distinguishable)
  • Web-based admin tools (phpMyAdmin export to gzip, Webmin) spawning sh for system tasks
  • Health-check scripts where nginx/php-fpm wrapper invokes curl to test upstream
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "healthcheck" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "composer" or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","imagemagick","gs","ffmpeg"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the parent process command line. If it shows the FPM worker handling a request, look at the access log entry within the matching second for that worker — confirm whether the URL was `pheditor.php?action=terminal`. Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host (Defender Live Response or network quarantine), kill the child shell PID and parent FPM worker, snapshot /var/www and /tmp before remediation. Step 3 — Hunt: Search the same host for .php files newly written under the webroot in the last 30 days (UC3), check the access log for GETs to any non-baseline .php returning 200 (UC4), and review outbound connections from the FPM worker UID for C2 candidates.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm", "apache2", "httpd", "nginx", "php")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","socat")
| where AccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","http","httpd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","socat")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","http","httpd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web Server Process Spawning Shell or Network Utility (Pheditor RCE / Webshell)
id: 7c4d2a8f-9b15-46e3-bf02-1e3a7c50d4b8
description: Detects php-fpm/apache/nginx spawning sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python or perl as the web-server user. Triggered by exploitation of Pheditor CVE-2026-48030 or any PHP webshell.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:

  - cve.2026.48030

  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:(php-fpm OR apache2 OR httpd OR nginx OR php) @process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash OR curl OR wget OR nc OR ncat OR python OR python3 OR perl OR socat) @user.name:(www-data OR apache OR nginx OR http OR httpd)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(php-fpm|apache2|httpd|nginx|php)/i ImageFileName=/(\/sh|\/bash|\/dash|\/curl|\/wget|\/nc|\/ncat|\/python3?|\/perl|\/socat)$/i UserName=/(www-data|apache|nginx|http|httpd)/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","apache2","httpd","nginx","php")) (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","socat")) Processes.user IN ("www-data","apache","nginx","http","httpd") by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

PHP webshell drop: php-fpm writing .php file under webroot with system()/eval() body AIInstallation High
Detects the Pheditor PoC step 5 — the dropper writes `<?php system($_GET["c"]);?>` to /var/www/html/shell.php. Any .php file created in a webroot by a php-fpm/apache UID is suspicious; cross-referencing the file body for system/exec/eval/passthru/shell_exec/$_GET/$_POST gates this to true webshells. Rationale: Article PoC literally writes `echo '<?php system($_GET["c"]);?>' > /var/www/html/shell.php`. Webroot path + .php extension + web-server-uid parent is article-grounded. The cmdline regex catches the shell-redirect form (`echo ... > shell.php`) even when the file create is signaled at the bash level rather than php-fpm.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WordPress / Drupal / Joomla auto-updates writing .php into the webroot via php-fpm (very common — needs allowlist by parent cmdline)
  • Composer/composer.phar installing PHP packages into vendor/ under the webroot
  • CI/CD agents (deploy as www-data) rolling out new releases
  • Pheditor itself being used legitimately to save a .php file (the admin UI does file management)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cron","composer install","composer update","drush","artisan") or FolderPath has_any ("/wp-content/upgrade/","/vendor/","/sites/default/files/php/"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Read the dropped .php file's content (Live Response `getfile`). If it contains `system($_`, `eval($_`, `passthru($_`, `shell_exec($_`, or `base64_decode($_`, treat as confirmed webshell. Step 2 — Contain: Quarantine the file, remove it from disk, isolate the host, and rotate any credentials stored in the same webroot's config (DB password, API keys). Step 3 — Hunt: Search the access log for GETs to the dropped file's name within the last 30 days (UC4), pivot on the parent FPM worker's earlier requests to find the exploit attempt (UC1), and check for any other .php files with anomalous SHA256 in the webroot.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/var/www/","/srv/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","/opt/pheditor")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","sh","bash")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","http","httpd")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("system($_","eval($_","passthru($_","shell_exec($_","<?php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "php"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/var/www/","/srv/www/","/usr/share/nginx/","/opt/pheditor")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","sh","bash")
| where ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","http","httpd")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("system($_","eval($_","passthru($_","shell_exec($_","<?php")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Pheditor-dropped webshell access: GET to .php with single-letter command parameter AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts post-drop interaction with the webshell from PoC step 5. The dropped shell takes `?c=<cmd>` (`curl http://TARGET/shell.php?c=id`). Surface any GET to a .php under the webroot with a short query parameter that maps to a known webshell convention (c, cmd, exec, x, do). Rationale: Article PoC step 5 shows `curl "http://TARGET/shell.php?c=id"`. The `?c=` convention is the literal exploit signature; `cmd/exec/x/do` are common webshell conventions that catch the same operator using a slightly different drop. Excluding `pheditor.php`, `index.php`, `wp-login.php` removes the typical legit short-param endpoints.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy PHP apps using `?c=category` or `?cmd=login` as legitimate routing parameters
  • WordPress plugins that take `?do=action` (Contact Form 7, WooCommerce admin endpoints)
  • Monitoring probes / synthetic checks hitting status.php with `?cmd=ping`
  • Internal developer testing the webshell-drop logic during a pentest
Suppression filter
| where not (cIP startswith "10." or cIP startswith "192.168." or csUriStem has_any ("/wp-content/","/admin/","/api/"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Open the matching .php file on the web server (Live Response). If it contains `system($_GET`, `eval($_GET`, or `passthru($_REQUEST` and is not part of the application's source tree, it's a webshell. Step 2 — Contain: Delete the file, block the source IP at the perimeter, snapshot the host, rotate the pheditor admin password (since the attacker authenticated first), and audit any DB credentials reachable from the web user. Step 3 — Hunt: Walk the access log for all 200-returning GETs to the same .php across the org's other web hosts, and pivot on the source IP for related auth events (Pheditor login attempts in the last 30 days).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod =~ "GET"
| where csUriStem endswith ".php"
| where csUriQuery matches regex @"(^|&)(c|cmd|exec|x|do)="
| where scStatus in ("200")
| where csUriStem !endswith_cs "/index.php"
| where csUriStem !endswith_cs "/pheditor.php"
| where csUriStem !endswith_cs "/wp-login.php"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus, csBytes, scBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Suspicious GET to .php with Short Command Parameter (Webshell Access)
id: e6c2b9d5-3f47-4a12-8d0b-58a9e4f12c7e
description: Detects HTTP GETs to a .php file with a short single-letter or known-webshell parameter (c, cmd, exec, x, do) returning 200. Triggered by access to webshells dropped via Pheditor CVE-2026-48030.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method: GET
  selection_php:
    cs-uri-stem|endswith: '.php'
  selection_param:
    cs-uri-query|re: '(^|&)(c|cmd|exec|x|do)='
  selection_status:
    sc-status: 200
  condition: all of selection_*
level: medium
(source:nginx.access OR source:apache.access) @http.method:GET @http.url:*.php* @http.status_code:200 (@http.url:*?c=* OR @http.url:*&c=* OR @http.url:*?cmd=* OR @http.url:*&cmd=* OR @http.url:*?exec=* OR @http.url:*?x=* OR @http.url:*?do=*) -@http.url:*wp-login.php* -@http.url:*pheditor.php* -@http.url:*index.php*
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.src) as src values(Web.http_user_agent) as ua values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.url="*.php*" (Web.url="*?c=*" OR Web.url="*?cmd=*" OR Web.url="*?exec=*" OR Web.url="*?x=*" OR Web.url="*?do=*" OR Web.url="*&c=*" OR Web.url="*&cmd=*") by Web.dest Web.url Web.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status=200 | rex field=url "/(?<phpfile>[^/]+\.php)" | search NOT phpfile IN ("index.php","pheditor.php","login.php","config.php","wp-login.php","wp-admin.php","admin.php")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.src) as src values(Web.http_user_agent) as ua values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET Web.url="*.php*" (Web.url="*?c=*" OR Web.url="*?cmd=*" OR Web.url="*?exec=*" OR Web.url="*?x=*" OR Web.url="*?do=*" OR Web.url="*&c=*" OR Web.url="*&cmd=*") by Web.dest Web.url Web.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status=200 | rex field=url "/(?<phpfile>[^/]+\.php)" | search NOT phpfile IN ("index.php","pheditor.php","login.php","config.php","wp-login.php","wp-admin.php","admin.php")
Web-server account (www-data) invoking privilege escalation utilities (sudo/su/setcap) AIActions on Objectives High
After Pheditor RCE drops the attacker to www-data, the natural next step is to escalate off the web user. Detect www-data/apache/nginx UID invoking sudo, su, pkexec, setcap, or chmod +s — none of which are TERMINAL_COMMANDS whitelist entries and none of which a normal web-server should ever run. Rationale: Article confirms post-exploit identity is `uid=33(www-data)`. www-data running sudo or pkexec is essentially never legitimate — there's no admin reason for the web user to escalate. Tying parent to php-fpm/apache/sh ensures the escalation chain traces back to a request-handling process, not e.g. an interactive console.
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1548.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration management agents (Ansible, Chef, Puppet) running as www-data temporarily to fix permissions — rare and usually documented
  • Web-based admin panels (Webmin, ISPConfig) that legitimately wrap sudoers — should be allowlisted by parent path
  • Composer post-install scripts running chmod (without +s) on bin directories — caught by the chmod +s gate
  • Maintenance crons that touch sudoers via the apache user (very uncommon)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","saltstack") or ProcessCommandLine has "sudoers.d/web-deploy")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the full parent chain — confirm parent traces back to php-fpm/apache and not an interactive ssh session. Identify which sudo target the attacker invoked (sudoers file + `-u` flag in the command). Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host, kill the privesc process tree, freeze the www-data shell session, and audit /etc/sudoers, /etc/sudoers.d/, and all setuid binaries (`find / -perm -4000 -type f`) for tampering. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the host for all www-data process activity in the last 14 days, look for new setuid binaries (UC3 file-event variant on /usr/bin/*), and check /etc/passwd/shadow modification timestamps for unauthorized account creation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","http","httpd")
| where FileName in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","setcap","chmod","passwd","newgrp")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","sh","bash","dash")
| where FileName != "chmod"
   or (FileName == "chmod" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(\+s|u\+s|[46]755|[46]777)")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername in~ ("www-data","apache","nginx","http","httpd")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","setcap","chmod","passwd","newgrp")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","apache2","httpd","nginx","sh","bash","dash")
| where TargetProcessName != "chmod"
   or (TargetProcessName == "chmod" and TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(\+s|u\+s|[46]755|[46]777)")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web Server User Invoking Privilege Escalation Utility
id: 1d8f5c92-7a3e-4b06-9c14-2e7a45b8e9f3
description: Detects www-data, apache or nginx UID running sudo, su, pkexec, setcap, or chmod +s — almost always post-exploitation following a webshell or RCE such as Pheditor CVE-2026-48030.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jvc5-6g7q-c843
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - attack.t1548.003
  - attack.t1548.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_user:
    User:
      - www-data
      - apache
      - nginx
      - http
      - httpd
  selection_image:

Blinding the Watchmen: Abusing Cloud Logging Services for Defense Evasion and Visibility

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-06-09 9 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Unit 42 research examines attack scenarios targeting cloud logging services. Learn how to defend against log manipulation and defense evasion. The post Blinding the Watchmen: Abusing Cloud Logging Services for Defense Evasion and Visibility appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1190 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] AWS CloudTrail StopLogging API invocation (logging disablement) · [LLM] AWS S3 DeleteBucket targeting a CloudTrail log destination bucket · [LLM] AWS CloudTrail DeleteTrail removing the trail configuration · [LLM] GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled via logging.sinks.update · [LLM] GCP log bucket deletion via logging.buckets.delete (DELETE_REQUESTED)
AWS CloudTrail StopLogging API invocation (logging disablement) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects invocation of the CloudTrail `StopLogging` API, which immediately halts log delivery from a trail to its S3 destination. The article identifies this as the most direct method to blind defenders; it requires only `cloudtrail:StopLogging` permission on the trail and typically precedes a larger attack. Rationale: Targets the article's explicitly named `cloudtrail:StopLogging` API (Technique 1). Filtering on `errorCode` absence ensures we catch only successful disablement; CallerType/CallerArn surface whether this came from a Root, IAMUser, or AssumedRole — Root or unexpected role identity is the high-fidelity pivot.
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised trail consolidation or migration to a new central account
  • Cost-optimisation deletion of duplicate trails by FinOps
  • IaC (Terraform/CloudFormation) tearing down ephemeral environment trails
  • Trail rotation as part of incident response evidence preservation
  • Account decommissioning closing out CloudTrail before account closure
Suppression filter
| where CallerArn !has_any ("role/TerraformExecutionRole", "role/CloudFormation", "AWSCloudFormationStackSetExecutionRole") and UserAgent !has_any ("cloudformation.amazonaws.com", "terraform")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the trail name from RequestParameters.name and confirm whether it is a primary security trail (multi-region/org trail) or a workload-specific one. Pull the caller's CallerArn and SourceIpAddress; check whether the call came from an approved IaC role/IP or an interactive session. 2. Contain: invoke `StartLogging` on the affected trail immediately; if the caller is unauthorised, revoke that principal's session tokens (`aws iam delete-access-key` / role session revocation policy) and rotate credentials. 3. Hunt: in the silent window (StopLogging → StartLogging) review GuardDuty findings, Config snapshots, VPC flow logs and any other parallel telemetry source for IAM privilege escalation, S3 data exfiltration, KMS key tampering, or new persistence (users, access keys, federation IdPs).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where Application in ("Amazon Web Services", "AWS")
| where ActionType =~ "StopLogging"
   or (ActionType has "StopLogging" and ObjectType has_any ("Trail","CloudTrail"))
| extend RawData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend TrailName = tostring(RawData.requestParameters.name),
         CallerType = tostring(RawData.userIdentity.type),
         CallerArn = tostring(RawData.userIdentity.arn),
         ErrorCode = tostring(RawData.errorCode)
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, CallerType, CallerArn, IPAddress, CountryCode, TrailName, ObjectName, UserAgent, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventName == "StopLogging"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend TrailName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).name)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityType, UserIdentityUserName, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, AwsRegion, TrailName, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AWS S3 DeleteBucket targeting a CloudTrail log destination bucket AIActions on Objectives High
Detects deletion of an S3 bucket that is — or recently was — the destination for a CloudTrail trail. The article describes attackers with `s3:DeleteBucket` (plus `s3:DeleteObject` to empty it) destroying the long-term forensic store; after deletion the trail's configuration shows the bucket is gone. Rationale: The article calls out `s3:DeleteBucket` + `s3:DeleteObject` against the trail destination as Technique 2, with explicit screenshot of the trail showing the destination bucket missing. Naming-pattern heuristics for log buckets are the article-specific signal; pair with a known-good list of log buckets in your environment for the highest fidelity.
ATT&CKT1485 T1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Retention migration moving logs to a new bucket then deleting the old one
  • Account decommissioning during an org-wide consolidation
  • Terraform/CDK refactor that recreates the log bucket under a new name
  • FinOps cleanup of stale buckets after a workload sunset
  • Disaster-recovery test bucket cleanup
Suppression filter
| where CallerArn !has_any ("role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole") and UserAgent !has_any ("cloudformation.amazonaws.com", "terraform", "control-tower")
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture BucketName, CallerArn, SourceIpAddress, UserAgent. Check whether the bucket was the active destination for any trail (`aws cloudtrail describe-trails` historical config) and whether a replacement bucket exists. Cross-reference with Config history. 2. Contain: revoke the caller's credentials/session if the action wasn't pre-approved, suspend the bucket-policy modification path, and check S3 versioning/object-lock to determine whether prior log objects can be recovered. 3. Hunt: timeline the window from last successful trail log delivery to bucket deletion; in that gap look at GuardDuty/VPC Flow/Config for IAM key creation, role assumption, exfil to public buckets, and any other Technique 1-5 indicators from the article.
let LogBucketHints = dynamic(["cloudtrail","audit","log-archive","-logs-","securitylogs","loggingbucket"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where Application in ("Amazon Web Services","AWS")
| where ActionType =~ "DeleteBucket"
| extend RawData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend BucketName = tolower(tostring(RawData.requestParameters.bucketName)),
         CallerType = tostring(RawData.userIdentity.type),
         CallerArn = tostring(RawData.userIdentity.arn),
         ErrorCode = tostring(RawData.errorCode)
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| where BucketName has_any (LogBucketHints)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, CallerType, CallerArn, IPAddress, CountryCode, BucketName, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc
let LogBucketHints = dynamic(["cloudtrail","audit","log-archive","-logs-","securitylogs","loggingbucket"]);
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventName == "DeleteBucket"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend BucketName = tolower(tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).bucketName))
| where BucketName has_any (LogBucketHints)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityType, UserIdentityArn, UserIdentityUserName, SourceIpAddress, AwsRegion, BucketName, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AWS CloudTrail DeleteTrail removing the trail configuration AIActions on Objectives High
Detects deletion of an entire CloudTrail trail via the `DeleteTrail` API — a step beyond StopLogging that destroys the trail's configuration including its S3/KMS/CloudWatch wiring. Unlike StopLogging this also removes evidence of how logging was originally configured, making restoration harder. Rationale: Reviewer-flagged: the article focuses on `StopLogging` but `DeleteTrail` is the related higher-impact API that removes the trail config altogether. Detection is a single-eventName match with success filter — extremely low FP; alert-worthy on any IAMUser/AssumedRole caller that isn't in a known IaC allowlist.
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IaC pipeline replacing a trail (DeleteTrail immediately followed by CreateTrail with same name)
  • Control Tower / Landing Zone account adoption renaming trails
  • Migration from individual-account trails to an org-wide trail
  • Retiring duplicate trails after central-trail rollout
  • Test account cleanup during sandbox tear-down
Suppression filter
| where CallerArn !has_any ("role/AWSControlTowerExecution", "role/OrganizationAccountAccessRole", "role/TerraformExecutionRole") and UserAgent !has_any ("cloudformation.amazonaws.com", "terraform", "control-tower")
Response runbook
1. Triage: was a replacement CreateTrail seen within ~5 minutes from the same caller? If yes and from an IaC role, likely benign rotation. If no replacement or a different caller, escalate. Capture CallerArn, SourceIpAddress, UserAgent. 2. Contain: re-create the trail with the prior configuration (pull from Config history if available) and re-enable logging; revoke caller's credentials if unauthorised. 3. Hunt: in the trail-blind window, pivot to alternative telemetry (Config, GuardDuty, VPC Flow, application logs, Defender for Cloud) for IAM persistence, KMS key changes, S3 data movement, federation-IdP creation, and any other Technique 1-5 indicators.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where Application in ("Amazon Web Services","AWS")
| where ActionType =~ "DeleteTrail"
| extend RawData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend TrailName = tostring(RawData.requestParameters.name),
         CallerType = tostring(RawData.userIdentity.type),
         CallerArn = tostring(RawData.userIdentity.arn),
         ErrorCode = tostring(RawData.errorCode)
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, CallerType, CallerArn, IPAddress, CountryCode, TrailName, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc
AWSCloudTrail
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where EventName == "DeleteTrail"
| where isempty(ErrorCode)
| extend TrailName = tostring(parse_json(RequestParameters).name)
| project TimeGenerated, EventName, UserIdentityType, UserIdentityUserName, UserIdentityArn, SourceIpAddress, AwsRegion, TrailName, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GCP Cloud Logging sink disabled via logging.sinks.update AIActions on Objectives High
Detects an attacker setting a Cloud Logging sink's `disabled` field to true via the `google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink` method — the GCP equivalent of CloudTrail StopLogging called out in the article. Once disabled, the sink stops routing matching log entries to their destination. Rationale: Targets the article's named GCP technique: `logging.sinks.update` permission used to set the sink's `disabled` field to true (Figure 1 in the article confirms the console message). Filter on `disabled:true` keeps this very low FP — most legitimate sink updates change filter expressions or destinations, not the disable flag.
ATT&CKT1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned cost-control pause of a high-volume sink
  • Sink destination migration where the old sink is disabled before deletion
  • SRE pausing a sink during BigQuery quota troubleshooting
  • Org Policy enforcement work that temporarily disables non-compliant sinks
  • Disaster recovery testing of sink failover
Suppression filter
| where Principal !has_any ("@cloudbuild", "@compute-system", "-terraform@", "@gcp-sa-") and Principal !endswith ".iam.gserviceaccount.com"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull Principal, CallerIp, ProjectId, SinkName, SinkDestination. Identify whether the sink routes security-relevant logs (Admin Activity, Data Access, VPC Flow) or low-value app logs. Check change-management for an approved maintenance window. 2. Contain: re-enable the sink (`gcloud logging sinks update <name> --no-disabled`); if the principal is unauthorised revoke its session and audit recently granted IAM bindings for `logging.sinks.update`. 3. Hunt: during the blind window cross-reference VPC Flow, GCP IAM bindings, Cloud KMS key changes, and Workspace audit for IdP/role abuse; review whether other sinks in the project were also disabled or rerouted.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where Application in ("Google Cloud Platform","Google Cloud")
| where ActionType has "UpdateSink" or ActionType =~ "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink"
| extend RawData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend SinkName = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.request.sink.name),
         SinkDestination = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.request.sink.destination),
         Disabled = tobool(RawData.protoPayload.request.sink.disabled),
         Principal = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail),
         CallerIp = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp),
         ProjectId = tostring(RawData.resource.labels.project_id)
| where Disabled == true
| project Timestamp, Principal, CallerIp, ProjectId, SinkName, SinkDestination, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Application in ("Google Cloud Platform","Google Cloud")
| where ActionType has "UpdateSink" or ActionType =~ "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink"
| extend RawData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend SinkName = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.request.sink.name),
         SinkDestination = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.request.sink.destination),
         Disabled = tobool(RawData.protoPayload.request.sink.disabled),
         Principal = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail),
         CallerIp = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp),
         ProjectId = tostring(RawData.resource.labels.project_id)
| where Disabled == true
| project TimeGenerated, Principal, CallerIp, ProjectId, SinkName, SinkDestination, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GCP log bucket deletion via logging.buckets.delete (DELETE_REQUESTED) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the `google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket` call against a Cloud Logging log bucket. As the article notes, the bucket enters a 7-day DELETE_REQUESTED state before destruction, giving defenders a window to restore — but the deletion itself is the high-fidelity defense-evasion signal. Rationale: Article Technique 2 (GCP variant): `logging.buckets.delete` permission used to delete a log bucket; deletion enters DELETE_REQUESTED state for 7 days. The methodName is a fixed string so this is a deterministic single-event alert. Principal filtering catches unauthorised users vs known IaC service accounts.
ATT&CKT1485 T1562.008
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioning a stale log bucket after migration to a central project
  • Terraform destroy of an ephemeral project's logging infrastructure
  • Org-wide log retention rework consolidating buckets
  • Cleanup of test/sandbox project buckets
  • Cost-control deletion of an unused secondary log bucket
Suppression filter
| where Principal !has "-terraform@" and Principal !endswith "@cloudbuild.gserviceaccount.com" and CallerIp !in ("35.235.240.0/20")
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture Principal, CallerIp, ProjectId, BucketResource. Because GCP holds the bucket in DELETE_REQUESTED for 7 days, immediate restoration is possible via `gcloud logging buckets undelete`. Determine whether the deleted bucket held security-relevant logs. 2. Contain: issue the undelete within the 7-day window; revoke the principal's session and audit recently granted `logging.admin` / `logging.bucketsAdmin` bindings. 3. Hunt: pivot to other techniques described in the article — was a sink also disabled (UpdateSink), is a parallel attacker-owned export sink siphoning logs to an external project, has the KMS CMEK for the bucket been rotated or revoked?
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where Application in ("Google Cloud Platform","Google Cloud")
| where ActionType has "DeleteBucket" and ActionType has "logging"
   or ActionType =~ "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket"
| extend RawData = parse_json(RawEventData)
| extend BucketResource = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.resourceName),
         Principal = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail),
         CallerIp = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp),
         ProjectId = tostring(RawData.resource.labels.project_id),
         ErrorCode = tostring(RawData.protoPayload.status.code)
| where ErrorCode in ("","0")
| project Timestamp, Principal, CallerIp, ProjectId, BucketResource, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)

description: Detects deletion of a Cloud Logging log bucket — destroys forensic evidence after a 7-day DELETE_REQUESTED period.

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18

  - attack.t1485
logsource:
  product: gcp
  service: gcp.audit
detection:

falsepositives:

level: high
source:gcp.audit @protoPayload.methodName:google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket -@protoPayload.status.code:(1 OR 7 OR 13 OR 16)
CLOUD
`gcp_pubsub` protoPayload.methodName="google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteBucket"
| rename protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail as principal, protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp as src_ip, protoPayload.resourceName as bucket_resource, resource.labels.project_id as project_id
| where NOT match(principal, "(?i)gserviceaccount\.com$") OR match(principal, "(?i)(compute@developer|cloudservices@cloudservices)\.gserviceaccount\.com")=false
